pericopes.text: I, Nephi, having been born of goodly parents, therefore I was taught somewhat in all the learning of my father; and having seen many afflictions in the course of my days—nevertheless, having been highly favored of the Lord in all my days; yea, having had a great knowledge of the goodness and the mysteries of God, therefore I make a record of my proceedings in my days;

links.text: And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.

provenance.route: Exodus 2:2 (Moses birth notice) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'Goodly' is a common KJV adjective — of cedars, cattle, garments, and persons — and 'goodly parents' may be nothing more than a conventional compliment.
provenance.significance: If the echo holds, Nephi casts himself as Moses in his opening six words, before any narrative has begun. That reading is not isolated: the pillar of fire arrives at 1:6, the borrowed praise at 1:14 is what Revelation 15:3 calls 'the song of Moses', and chapter 17 argues Nephi's authority from Moses at length. The first sentence would then be setting the type the book spends twenty-two chapters filling.

links.note: 'I, Nephi, having been born of goodly parents' opens the book. The KJV's one memorable use of 'goodly' in a birth notice is Exodus 2:2, where Moses' mother 'saw him that he was a goodly child' — the sentence that launches the Exodus. Nephi's clause shares the adjective and the birth setting while transferring the epithet from the child to the parents, which is what an allusion under compression tends to do. Proposed here as a deliberate risk: the verbal contact is one word, and the case rests on the Moses typology that demonstrably governs the rest of 1 Nephi.
links.whyNot: One shared adjective and no shared syntax. 'Goodly' appears throughout the KJV in wholly unrelated settings, and a reader who did not already expect Moses typology would have no reason to hear Exodus 2:2 here. The machine streams did not propose this and could not have; it is a reading imported from the book's later chapters, and it should be the first record struck if the cluster it depends on fails to hold up across 1 Nephi 17.

pericopes.text: yea, I make a record in the language of my father, which consists of the learning of the Jews and the language of the Egyptians.
And I know that the record which I make, to be true; and I make it with mine own hand; and I make it according to my knowledge.

links.text: I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.

provenance.route: Pauline autograph formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: A Pauline epistolary formula in the mouth of a pre-exilic Israelite. The formula is ordinary enough that it cannot prove the case alone, but the project's business is to put such things on the table.

links.note: Nephi authenticates his record exactly where Paul authenticates his letter: 'I make it with mine own hand' answers 'I Paul have written it with mine own hand.' The function matches as well as the wording — both are first-person guarantees of an autograph attached to a claim that the document is trustworthy, and Nephi's stands one clause after 'I know that the record which I make, to be true.'
links.whyNot: 'With mine own hand' is a commonplace of the KJV's epistolary idiom (1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11, Colossians 4:18, 2 Thessalonians 3:17), not a phrase peculiar to Philemon, and no second marker ties Nephi to that letter rather than to the formula at large. Kept at moderate because the FUNCTION matches as precisely as the wording — both are first-person guarantees of an autograph attached to a claim that the document is trustworthy — and a Pauline authentication formula in a pre-exilic colophon is worth putting on the table even undecided.

pericopes.text: For it came to pass, in the commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, (my father Lehi having dwelt at Jerusalem in all his days;) and in that same year there came many prophets, prophesying unto the people, that they must repent, or the great city Jerusalem must be destroyed.

links.text: And it came to pass the same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, and in the fifth month, that Hananiah the son of Azur the prophet, which was of Gibeon, spake unto me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying,

provenance.route: Jeremiah's dating formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: The synchronism may be a generic biblical date formula rather than a borrowing from Jeremiah in particular; regnal dating by 'the Nth year of the reign of X king of Judah' is the standard idiom of Kings and Chronicles as well.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon opens by dating itself in the exact idiom of the prophet whose ministry it presupposes. Lehi is made Jeremiah's contemporary in the first sentence of narrative, and the shared formula is the instrument that does it.

links.note: 'The commencement of the first year of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah' reproduces the frame of Jeremiah's own datelines — 'in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah' at both Jeremiah 28:1 and 49:34, with Jeremiah 1:3 supplying the same regnal anchor for the prophet's own call. The convergence is not merely verbal: 1 Nephi 1:4 goes on to say that 'there came many prophets, prophesying unto the people, that they must repent, or the great city Jerusalem must be destroyed,' which is Jeremiah's message, and the chapter ends with Lehi persecuted for delivering it, which is Jeremiah's biography. The dateline places Lehi inside Jeremiah's book.

pericopes.text: Wherefore it came to pass, that my father Lehi, as he went forth, prayed unto the Lord, yea, even with all his heart, in behalf of his people.

And it came to pass, as he prayed unto the Lord, there came a pillar of fire and dwelt upon a rock before him; and he saw and heard much; and because of the things which he saw and heard, he did quake and tremble exceedingly.

links.text: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:

provenance.route: Exodus theophany → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: Lehi's prophetic call is narrated in the vocabulary of the Exodus, which is the typology the whole of 1 Nephi will run on: a family led out of a doomed land, through a wilderness, across water, to a promised land. The pillar of fire is where that typology starts.

links.note: 'There came a pillar of fire and dwelt upon a rock before him' takes the Exodus guidance-theophany and relocates it from the nation to a single man. 'Pillar of fire' occurs six times in the KJV (Exodus 13:21, 13:22, 14:24; Numbers 14:14; Nehemiah 9:12, 9:19) and in every case it is the LORD leading Israel out of Egypt — the phrase carries no other biblical sense. Applying it to a private call vision in Jerusalem is a deliberate transfer, and it announces the Exodus pattern that 1 Nephi 17 will make explicit when Nephi argues his own case from Moses.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he returned to his own house at Jerusalem; and he cast himself upon his bed, being overcome with the spirit and the things which he had seen;

links.text: Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.

provenance.route: Prophetic collapse type-scene (Daniel, Ezekiel) → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: The claim here is generic, not verbal: Lehi is being placed in a recognized class of visionary. This is what the `figural` type is for — a link that is real at the level of narrative form and absent at the level of wording.

links.note: 'He cast himself upon his bed, being overcome with the spirit' is the standard aftermath of a major vision in the prophetic books: Daniel 10:8–9 loses all strength and falls into a deep sleep on his face, and Ezekiel 3:15 sits astonished seven days. The sequence — vision, physical collapse, later report — is a type-scene, and 1 Nephi 1:7 occupies its middle term precisely.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact whatever with Daniel or Ezekiel here; the machine streams did not propose this link and could not have. The judgment rests entirely on narrative form, which means it is weaker evidence for KJV dependence than any of the verbal links in this chapter and should never be counted toward the KJV-specificity argument.

links.text: So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees,

provenance.alternative: The prophetic-collapse reading (Daniel 10:8–9, recorded separately at this verse) accounts for Lehi's posture without needing Elijah at all.
provenance.significance: Both readings can stand at once. Daniel supplies the type-scene — vision, collapse, report; Elijah supplies the wording. If the Elijah echo is heard, Lehi's private collapse is coloured by the most public prophetic contest in the Hebrew Bible, which is the situation Lehi walks into eleven verses later.

links.note: 'He cast himself upon his bed' shares its verb phrase with Elijah on Carmel, who 'cast himself down upon the earth' — the KJV's reflexive 'cast himself' is not common, and both men are prophets going prone immediately after an encounter with God. Recorded alongside, not instead of, the Daniel type-scene at the same verse: the two are different claims about the same clause, one verbal and one formal.
links.whyNot: The objects differ — 'upon his bed' against 'upon the earth' — and so do the functions: Elijah is deliberately assuming a posture of prayer to summon rain, Lehi is involuntarily overcome. A shared two-word reflexive is thin, and the machine proposed it on that basis alone.

pericopes.text: and being thus overcome with the spirit, he was carried away in a vision, even that he saw the Heavens open; and he thought he saw God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels in the attitude of singing and praising their God.

links.text: And he said, Hear thou therefore the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.

provenance.route: Divine-council throne vision (Micaiah, Isaiah, Daniel) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: Lehi is given the credential that authenticates a true prophet in the Hebrew Bible: he has stood in the divine council and seen the throne. The Book of Mormon is claiming for Lehi the precise standing that 1 Kings 22 uses to distinguish Micaiah from the four hundred false prophets. Confirmed by Hardy's Maxwell Institute Study Edition apparatus, which notes that these twenty-one words recur verbatim at Alma 36:22, where Alma explicitly models his own conversion vision on 'our father Lehi['s]' — the clearest possible case of Hays's recurrence criterion (CONVENTIONS.md §3a): a later Nephite author read this scene as formulaic throne-vision language and reused it deliberately, which is independent evidence that the scene functions as a type in the book's own internal reception, not only in ours.

links.note: 'He thought he saw God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels' is the divine-council vision in its classic form. 'Sitting on/upon his throne' with the heavenly host in attendance occurs in the KJV at 1 Kings 22:19 and its parallel 2 Chronicles 18:18, and the enthronement half at Isaiah 6:1; the innumerable attendants come from Daniel 7:10 ('thousand thousands ministered unto him') and Revelation 5:11. Micaiah's vision is the closest: it shares the seated Lord, the throne, and the surrounding host, and it functions as Micaiah's warrant for contradicting the official prophets — which is exactly the position Lehi occupies eleven verses later. That this exact wording recurs, unprompted, in Alma's account of his own vision two books later (Alma 36:22, 'God sitting upon his throne, surrounded with numberless concourses of angels, in the attitude of singing and praising their God') is independent confirmation that the Book of Mormon itself treats this as a fixed formula for a throne-vision, which is exactly the biblical type this link claims.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 1.8: 'The twenty-one words "saw God . . . praising their God" are quoted exactly at Alma 36.22.'

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he saw one descending out of the midst of Heaven, and he beheld that his lustre was above that of the sun at noon-day;
and he also saw twelve others following him, and their brightness did exceed that of the stars in the firmament;

links.text: And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

provenance.route: The Twelve → Book of Mormon vision imagery
provenance.alternative: The twelve may be read as the heavenly host or as the twelve tribes rather than the apostolic college, in which case no New Testament dependence is involved at all.
provenance.significance: If the twelve are the apostles, then a vision dated to 600 BC contains the apostolic college — the same anachronism that 1 Nephi 11:34–36 and 13:26 make explicit and verbal. The interpretive weight rests on those later verses, not on this one.

links.note: 'He also saw twelve others following him' comes immediately after 'one descending out of the midst of Heaven' whose brightness exceeds the sun. Read forward, the vision identifies itself: at 1 Nephi 11:34–36 and 13:26 the text speaks of 'the twelve apostles of the Lamb,' which is a verbatim borrowing from Revelation 21:14, and applies it to the same figures. 1 Nephi 1:10 is the first, unglossed appearance of that group.
links.whyNot: Taken by itself this verse has no verbal contact with Revelation 21:14 or any other New Testament text — it says only 'twelve others.' The identification is imported from later chapters of 1 Nephi rather than established here, so the link is structural and provisional; a reader who declines the forward reference is left with nothing to adjudicate.

pericopes.text: and they came down and went forth upon the face of the earth; and the first came and stood before my father, and gave unto him a Book, and bade him that he should read.
And it came to pass that as he read, he was filled with the spirit of the Lord,

and he read, saying, Wo, wo unto Jerusalem! for I have seen thine abominations; yea, and many things did my father read concerning Jerusalem—that it should be destroyed, and the inhabitants thereof, many should perish by the sword, and many should be carried away captive into Babylon.

links.text: I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, and thine abominations on the hills in the fields. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?

provenance.significance: Lehi's book — the one handed him in vision — opens with Jeremiah's own indictment of Jerusalem. The vision authenticates itself by speaking in the voice of the prophet then active in the city.

links.note: The three elements of Lehi's reading are all present in a single verse of Jeremiah, and in the same order: the woe over Jerusalem ('Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem!' ~ 'Wo, wo unto Jerusalem!'), the first-person sight of her sins ('I have seen thine adulteries … and thine abominations' ~ 'for I have seen thine abominations'), and the coming judgement. The Book of Mormon takes 'abominations' — Jeremiah's second noun — and drops 'adulteries,' which is the more graphic term; the substitution is characteristic of the way the text handles Jeremiah's sexual imagery elsewhere. The machine stream found only the four-word run 'I have seen thine'; the strength of the case is the co-occurrence of all three elements in one verse, which no single n-gram could surface.

links.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the remnant of the people that remained in the city, and those that fell away, that fell to him, with the rest of the people that remained.

provenance.other: Modern versions render the same Hebrew as 'carried into exile' (ESV, NIV), which shares no wording with the Book of Mormon here.
provenance.significance: A five-word run reproducing the unique KJV phrasing of the event Lehi is predicting. This is the strongest KJV-specific claim in the chapter after 1:14: the wording is available in English only from the Authorized Version's idiom of 'carrying away captive.'

links.note: 'Many should be carried away captive into Babylon' reproduces 'carried away captive into Babylon' exactly. The phrase occurs precisely once in the entire KJV — at Jeremiah 39:9, in the narrative of the fall of Jerusalem — which makes it rarity-decisive rather than formulaic. Lehi is made to predict, in the historian's own later words, the deportation that Jeremiah 39 records as having happened.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when my father had read and saw many great and marvellous things, he did exclaim many things unto the Lord; such as, Great and marvellous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty! Thy throne is high in the Heavens, and thy power, and goodness, and mercy is over all the inhabitants of the earth; and because thou art merciful, thou wilt not suffer those who come unto thee that they shall perish!

links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: The Geneva Bible (1560) reads very nearly the same at this verse, so this passage on its own does not separate KJV from Geneva dependence. Recorded as a qualification, not a disqualification: the wording is the Authorized Version's as the Book of Mormon's readers would have met it.
provenance.significance: A prophet dated to 600 BC praises God in the words of a Christian apocalypse written around AD 95, in English. This is the chapter's central anachronism and the clearest instance in 1 Nephi of the phenomenon the whole catalogue exists to document. There is also a metaleptic gain (Hays 2016, Introduction): recover the context of Revelation 15:3 and the borrowed words turn out to be introduced there as 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Lehi therefore opens a book that will run on Exodus typology from 1:6 onward — and that will argue itself from Moses at length in chapter 17 — by praising God in what the source text labels the song of Moses. Neither text states the connection; only the link does.

links.note: 'Great and marvellous are thy works, O Lord God Almighty' reproduces Revelation 15:3 word for word across six words, adding only the vocative 'O' — which itself appears in the same formula at Revelation 11:17 ('O LORD God Almighty'), so the composite reading is likely. 'Great and marvellous' occurs twice in the KJV and both times in Revelation 15 (verses 1 and 3); nowhere else in the Bible. The 1830 text spells it 'marvellous,' matching the KJV's own orthography, and later editions modernized it to 'marvelous' — the first edition preserves the borrowing more visibly than the current text does. At six identical words the passage falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a 'literal quotation' and so is not one of his 36; by the taxonomy used here, a complete clause reproduced verbatim from a verse that is its only biblical home is a quotation regardless of length.

pericopes.text: And after this manner was the language of my father in the praising of his God; for his soul did rejoice, and his whole heart was filled, because of the things which he had seen; yea, which the Lord had shewn unto him.

And now I, Nephi, do not make a full account of the things which my father hath written, for he hath written many things which he saw in visions and in dreams; and he also hath written many things which he prophesied and spake unto his children, of which I shall not make a full account;

but I shall make an account of my proceedings in my days—Behold I make an abridgment of the record of my father, upon plates which I have made with mine own hands; wherefore, after that I have abridged the record of my father, then will I make an account of mine own life.

Therefore, I would that ye should know that after the Lord had shewn so many marvellous things unto my father Lehi, yea, concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, behold he went forth among the people, and began to prophesy and to declare unto them concerning the things which he had both seen and heard.

And it came to pass that the Jews did mock him because of the things which he testified of them; for he truly testified of their wickedness and their abominations; and he testified that the things which he saw and heard, and also the things which he read in the Book, manifested plainly of the coming of a Messiah, and also the redemption of the world.

links.text: Also day by day, from the first day unto the last day, he read in the book of the law of God. And they kept the feast seven days; and on the eighth day was a solemn assembly, according unto the manner.

provenance.route: Nehemiah 8 (Ezra's public reading) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'He read in the book' may be simply the plainest way in KJV English to say that someone read a book, with no scene behind it.
provenance.significance: Read as an echo, the interest is in the inversion. Nehemiah 8 is the paradigm scene of Israel receiving the book: the people gather 'as one man', 'the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law', and they weep and obey. 1 Nephi 1 runs the same scene backwards — a man reads a book given him by heaven, testifies from it, and the Jews mock him and seek his life. The Book of Mormon's opening thereby stages Israel failing the test Nehemiah records Israel passing.

links.note: Lehi 'testified that the things which he saw and heard, and also the things which he read in the Book, manifested plainly of the coming of a Messiah.' The phrase 'read in the book' matches Nehemiah 8:18's 'he read in the book of the law of God', and the surrounding scene matches more than the phrase does: a divinely given book read aloud in Jerusalem before the assembled people, with the people's reaction as the point of the episode in both cases. What differs is the reaction, and that difference is the reading.
links.whyNot: Four ordinary words, and the machine proposed it on that basis. Lehi's reading is visionary and private in origin where Ezra's is liturgical and public, and the 'scene' correspondence depends on treating 1 Nephi 1:11–19 as a unit rather than on anything in verse 19 itself. A reader who declines the inversion is left with a commonplace.

pericopes.text: And when the Jews heard these things, they were angry with him; yea, even as with the prophets of old, whom they had cast out and stoned and slain; and they also sought his life, that they might take it away. But behold, I, Nephi, will shew unto you that the tender mercies of the Lord is over all them whom he hath chosen, because of their faith, to make them mighty even unto the power of deliverance.

links.text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

provenance.alternative: The machine streams proposed Proverbs 12:10 on the strength of a longer contiguous string; see the exclusion register for why that reading fails.
provenance.other: 'Tender mercies' is the KJV's rendering of raḥămê; modern versions read 'compassion' or 'mercy' and lose the phrase entirely.
provenance.significance: Nephi's thesis statement for the whole book — the sentence he uses to say what his record is about — is built on the Psalter's formula for divine goodness, in the KJV's wording.

links.note: 'The tender mercies of the Lord is over all them whom he hath chosen' joins two KJV elements that occur together nowhere else. 'Tender mercies' appears eleven times in the KJV, ten of them in the Psalms; 'are/is over all' as a predicate appears in only two verses in the whole Bible (Psalm 145:9 and Romans 9:5). Psalm 145:9 is the single verse where both meet: 'his tender mercies are over all his works.' Nephi keeps the subject and the predicate and substitutes the object — 'all them whom he hath chosen' for 'all his works' — which narrows a statement about creation into a statement about election, and that narrowing is the point of his sentence. Note also that the 1830 text reads 'is over all' where the KJV reads 'are'; the 1920 edition corrected it to 'are,' moving the Book of Mormon closer to its source than the first edition had been.

links.text: Remember, O LORD, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses; for they have been ever of old.

provenance.route: The Psalter's 'tender mercies' formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: Psalm 145:9 alone accounts for Nephi's full sentence and is recorded separately at this verse; this record makes the broader claim that the phrase itself is a Psalter formula the Book of Mormon has absorbed.
provenance.other: 'Tender mercies' is the KJV's rendering of raḥămîm; modern versions read 'compassion' or 'mercy' and the collocation disappears.
provenance.significance: Nephi is not only borrowing one verse but writing inside a Psalms idiom. That matters for the thesis statement of his whole record: the sentence in which he tells us what his book is about reaches for the Psalter's characteristic vocabulary for divine goodness.

links.note: 'Tender mercies' occurs eleven times in the KJV and ten of them are in the Psalms — the one exception, Proverbs 12:10, inverts the sense and is rejected in the exclusion register. This is a phrase family rather than a single source, and the Book of Mormon uses it more than once: 1 Nephi 8:8 has 'according to the multitude of his tender mercies', which reproduces the fuller formula of Psalm 51:1 and 69:16 ('according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies'). Recurrence across the book is itself part of the case (compare Hays's third criterion), and it is why this record stands alongside the Psalm 145:9 link rather than being absorbed into it.

pericopes.text: For behold it came to pass that the Lord spake unto my father, yea, even in a dream, and sayeth unto him, Blessed art thou Lehi, because of the things which thou hast done; and because thou hast been faithful and declared unto this people the things which I commanded thee, behold they seek to take away thy life.

links.text: Therefore thus saith the LORD of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the LORD, that thou die not by our hand:

provenance.route: Jeremiah's persecution oracles → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'Seek thy life' is a standing KJV idiom for a lethal threat and occurs in ten verses (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, Jeremiah, Romans); the phrase alone points at no single one.
provenance.significance: The clause that ends chapter 1 ('the Jews … sought his life') and the clause that opens chapter 2 are the same clause, and it is Jeremiah's. What Jeremiah 11:21 supplies is not just the idiom but the situation: a prophet told by the LORD, in the LORD's own voice, that named men intend to kill him for prophesying. The Book of Mormon's plot begins where Jeremiah's does.

links.note: Divine speech informing a prophet that he is a marked man: 'behold they seek to take away thy life.' The idiom is widespread, but four of its ten KJV occurrences are Jeremiah's, the tightest is Jeremiah 11:21, and the frame around 1 Nephi 2:1 is Jeremiah's frame throughout — a Zedekiah dateline at 1:4, prophets preaching Jerusalem's destruction at 1:4, the prophet mocked and threatened at 1:19-20. Note also the direction of the divine counsel. Jeremiah is told to stay; Lehi is told to go. The Book of Mormon makes its opening move by taking Jeremiah's premise and reversing his outcome.

links.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: 'Blessed art thou' occurs in five KJV verses (Psalm 119:12, Ecclesiastes 10:17, Matthew 16:17, Luke 1:28, 42). Only Matthew 16:17 attaches it to a personal name in the vocative.
provenance.significance: Twice in one chapter the Lord opens a speech with 'Blessed art thou, <name>, because …' — to Lehi at 2:1 and to Nephi at 2:19. In the KJV the construction belongs to Peter's confession, where the blessing is specifically for having received what flesh and blood could not reveal. Both Book of Mormon uses reward exactly that: Lehi for declaring what he was shown, Nephi for believing it.

links.note: Of the five KJV verses reading 'Blessed art thou,' one addresses a named man and gives the ground of the blessing in a because-clause: Matthew 16:17. 1 Nephi 2:1 and 2:19 both reproduce that shape — vocative name, then 'because of.' The doubling matters: a formula used once could be coincidence, but the Lord's two direct addresses in this chapter are both cast in it, which is what a borrowed formula looks like in use.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord commanded my father, even in a dream, that he should take his family and depart into the wilderness.

links.text: And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.

provenance.route: Matthew's flight-into-Egypt sequence → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: Dream-warnings are common in both testaments (Genesis 31:10-13, Genesis 46:2-4, Matthew 27:19), and a command to flee an assassination plot needs no literary model.
provenance.significance: The sequence, not the wording, is what carries this. Warning in a dream · take the family · depart · because they seek the life. Matthew built that sequence over Exodus 4:19 ('all the men are dead which sought thy life'), and Matthew 2:20 quotes it. If 1 Nephi 2:1-2 is reading Matthew, it is reading a passage that is itself already a reading of Moses — which is the same double movement the pillar of fire at 1:6 and the borrowed 'song of Moses' at 1:14 are making.

links.note: Four elements in four clauses, in Matthew's order: the Lord speaks 'in a dream' (2:1), the addressee is told his life is sought (2:1), he is commanded to 'take his family' (2:2), and he departs (2:2, 2:4). Matthew 2:13 has the angel appear 'in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee,' with Herod's threat as the stated reason; Matthew 2:20 supplies 'they are dead which sought the young child's life.' The verbal contact is thin — 'in a dream' is the only phrase held in common — so this is proposed on sequence and situation.
links.whyNot: Two words of shared wording. Every element of the sequence has an Old Testament precedent available on the text's own chronology, and Exodus 4:19 alone would account for the life-seeking clause without Matthew. Kept at moderate because the four elements arrive in Matthew's order and in four consecutive clauses, which sequence alone rarely does by accident.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he was obedient unto the word of the Lord, wherefore he did as the Lord commanded him.

links.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.

provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:8-9 is the chapter's blueprint, not one of its ornaments. Called to go out · obeyed · left an inheritance behind · sojourned dwelling in tabernacles · in the land of promise · by faith. 1 Nephi 2 runs those clauses in order: obedient (2:3), left the land of his inheritance (2:4), dwelt in a tent (2:15), because of thy faith (2:19), a land of promise (2:20). The single KJV occurrence of the phrase 'land of promise' at Hebrews 11:9 (see 2:20) is what turns a family resemblance into a demonstrable one.

links.note: 'He was obedient unto the word of the Lord' is the hinge of Hebrews 11:8 — Abraham 'called to go out … obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went' — and Lehi likewise departs before he is told where. The elements Hebrews 11:8-9 strings together are the elements 1 Nephi 2 strings together, in the same order, and one of them ('land of promise') exists in exactly one KJV verse. Catalogued here at 2:3 as the head of that cluster; see 2:4, 2:15, 2:19 and 2:20 for its other members.

links.text: And Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded them, so did they.

provenance.route: Pentateuchal obedience refrain → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: This is the Torah's standing formula rather than any one verse's property; eight KJV verses read 'did as the LORD commanded' and no single one is identifiable as the source.
provenance.significance: The formula is reserved in the Pentateuch for Noah, Moses, and Aaron carrying out a divine instruction that will save or constitute a people. Lehi receives it in his third verse.

links.note: 'He did as the Lord commanded him' is the Pentateuch's refrain of executed obedience — Exodus 7:6 of Moses and Aaron, Genesis 6:22 of Noah building the ark, and six more in Leviticus and Numbers. The wording is not distinctive enough to name a source verse and is recorded as a formula rather than a quotation, but the formula is not neutral: it is what the Torah says about the men who obey the instruction that preserves the line.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he departed into the wilderness.— And he left his house, and the land of his inheritance, and his gold, and his silver, and his precious things, and took nothing with him save it were his family, and provisions, and tents, and he departed into the wilderness;

links.text: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee:

provenance.route: The call of Abram → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: Every departure narrative in Israel's scripture is measured against Genesis 12. What 1 Nephi 2:4 adds to the pattern is an inventory — house, land of inheritance, gold, silver, precious things — which reads as an answer to the question Genesis leaves open, namely what it costs to obey. Abram takes 'the substance that they had gathered' with him (Genesis 12:5); Lehi takes nothing.

links.note: Lehi leaves house, land of inheritance, and possessions at a divine command, for an unnamed destination that will turn out to be a promised land. That is Genesis 12:1 in outline, and the outline is filled in the same order: the leaving (2:4), the journey (2:5-6), the altar (2:7), the promise of a land (2:20). The pointed departure from the model is that Abram carries his substance and Lehi abandons his — the gold and silver of 2:4 will be sent back for in chapter 3 and refused as a price for the plates, which makes the inventory here a set-up rather than a flourish.

links.text: And every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.

provenance.route: The hundredfold saying → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: The list form ('his house, and the land of his inheritance, and his gold, and his silver') is ordinary Hebrew inventory style and needs no Gospel model.
provenance.significance: If the saying is in play, the promise attached to it is too: those who forsake houses and lands 'shall receive an hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.' 1 Nephi 2:20 answers with an inheritance — 'a land which I have prepared for you' — sixteen verses later. The exchange the Gospel promises is the exchange the chapter transacts.

links.note: The verse is built as a renunciation list of exactly the kind the Synoptics use: house first, then lands, then goods, all left for the word's sake. Matthew 19:29 and its parallels are the KJV's version of that list. Proposed as an echo rather than an allusion because no phrase is reproduced; what is shared is the form and the logic — abandonment now against inheritance later — and the chapter does supply the inheritance.

pericopes.text: and he came down by the borders near the shore of the Red Sea; and he travelled in the wilderness, in the borders, which was nearer the Red Sea; and he did travel in the wilderness with his family, which consisted of my mother, Sariah, and my elder brothers, which were Laman, Lemuel and Sam.

links.text: And king Solomon made a navy of ships in Eziongeber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom.

provenance.other: 'The shore of the Red sea' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Red Sea itself is everywhere in Exodus, but always as something crossed or drowned in, never as a shore travelled along.
provenance.significance: The geography is doing typological work in reverse. Israel comes out of Egypt to the Red Sea and crosses it going toward the land of promise; Lehi leaves the land of promise and travels down to the Red Sea, in the wrong direction, at the start of a book that will end by crossing an ocean. The one KJV verse that describes travel *along* that shore rather than through those waters is a shipbuilding verse, which is where 1 Nephi is going too (17:8).

links.note: 'He came down by the borders near the shore of the Red Sea.' The phrase 'the shore of the Red sea' is unique in the KJV to 1 Kings 9:26, Solomon's shipyard at Ezion-geber — the one biblical passage that treats that coastline as a place a party of Israelites travels to rather than a barrier God parts. The link is verbal and slight; its interest is that the chapter's Exodus machinery is running backwards here, and the source verse is about building ships.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when he had travelled three days in the wilderness, he pitched his tent in a valley beside a river of water.

links.text: So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water.

provenance.other: 'Three days in the wilderness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The related 'three days' journey into the wilderness' occurs at Exodus 3:18, 5:3 and 8:27, always as the distance Israel asks Pharaoh for in order to sacrifice.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is exact and the outcome is inverted. Exodus 15:22: three days in the wilderness, and found no water. 1 Nephi 2:6: three days in the wilderness, and he pitches his tent 'in a valley beside a river of water.' Then, in the next verse, Lehi does what Israel wanted the three days for in the first place (Exodus 3:18, 5:3) and sacrifices. The Book of Mormon takes Exodus's failed march and completes it, with the water present and the offering made.

links.note: A five-word run reproducing the only KJV verse containing it, in a narrative that has just come from the Red Sea, as Exodus 15:22 has. What makes this more than a phrase match is what happens on either side of it. Israel's three days end in thirst; Lehi's end at a river. And the errand Moses repeatedly requests three days in the wilderness for — 'let us go, we pray thee, three days' journey into the desert, and sacrifice unto the LORD our God' — is exactly what 1 Nephi 2:7 then narrates. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; recorded here as an allusion.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he built an altar of stones, and he made an offering unto the Lord, and gave thanks unto the Lord our God.

links.text: And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Bethel, and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the LORD, and called upon the name of the LORD.

provenance.route: The patriarchal tent-and-altar formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: Building an altar on arriving somewhere is what everyone in Genesis does, and the two verses need no single model.
provenance.significance: Genesis 12:8 and 26:25 are the two KJV verses that put pitching a tent and building an altar in one sentence, and both are moments when a patriarch takes possession of a place he has been promised but does not own. 1 Nephi 2:6-7 reproduces the pair in the same order, then names the valley and the river after his sons (2:8-10) — which is the other half of the patriarchal formula, the naming that stakes a claim.

links.note: The tent goes up in 2:6 and the altar in 2:7: 'he pitched his tent in a valley beside a river of water … he built an altar of stones, and he made an offering unto the Lord, and gave thanks unto the Lord our God.' Both KJV verses that pair those two acts are patriarchal arrival scenes — Abram at Bethel (Genesis 12:8) and Isaac at Beersheba (Genesis 26:25), each adding 'and called upon the name of the LORD,' for which Lehi's 'gave thanks unto the Lord our God' stands. The machine stream reached only the altar's stones; the pairing is what identifies the source.

links.text: And there shalt thou build an altar unto the LORD thy God, an altar of stones: thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them.

provenance.other: 'An altar of stones' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 27 is the altar Israel is to build on entering the land, at the covenant renewal on Ebal. Lehi builds his on leaving it. The unhewn stones are the point of the Deuteronomic law — an altar no tool has touched — and 1 Nephi's phrase carries that specification into a wilderness where no tool would have been available anyway.

links.note: 'He built an altar of stones' reproduces the exact phrase of Deuteronomy 27:5, the KJV's only occurrence, where it names the unhewn altar commanded for the entry into Canaan (cf. Exodus 20:25, 'thou shalt not build it of hewn stone'; Joshua 8:31, where the command is carried out). Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and the situation is inverted — Deuteronomy legislates an altar for arrival, Lehi builds one for departure — but the wording is the KJV's and belongs to one verse.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he called the name of the river Laman, and it emptied into the Red Sea; and the valley was in the borders near the mouth thereof.

And when my father saw that the waters of the river emptied into the fountain of the Red Sea, he spake unto Laman, saying: O that thou mightest be like unto this river, continually running into the fountain of all righteousness.

links.text: O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea:

provenance.other: 'O that thou' opens ten KJV verses; 'O that thou hadst' opens one. Isaiah 48:18 is also the only KJV verse that puts a wish-formula, commandments, a river, and righteousness in a single sentence.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most consequential link because of where it recurs. Lehi rebukes his two eldest sons in the words of Isaiah 48:18, and twenty chapters later Nephi transcribes Isaiah 48 entire, so that at 1 Nephi 20:18 the family reads out, as scripture, the verse their father had already spoken over them at the river. The catalogue can show the same text arriving twice by two different routes — once as a father's wish, once as a quoted prophecy — which is precisely Hays's recurrence criterion doing work.

links.note: Lehi's two blessings are the two halves of Isaiah 48:18. To Laman: 'O that thou mightest be like unto this river, continually running into the fountain of all righteousness' — Isaiah's wish-formula, his river, his righteousness. To Lemuel in the next verse: 'firm, and steadfast, and immovable in keeping the commandments of the Lord' — Isaiah's commandments. Isaiah's sentence laments an obedience that did not happen; Lehi's speech is a wish that it still might, addressed to the two sons of whom the book has just said they murmured. Both wishes fail, and Isaiah 48 is read aloud to them again in chapter 20.

pericopes.text: And he also spake unto Lemuel: O that thou mightest be like unto this valley, firm, and steadfast, and immovable in keeping the commandments of the Lord.

links.text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Unmoveable' occurs in two KJV verses (Acts 27:41, of a ship's bow stuck fast; 1 Corinthians 15:58). Only 1 Corinthians 15:58 pairs it with 'stedfast', and it does so in the same asyndetic run of adjectives that 1 Nephi 2:10 uses.
provenance.significance: A Pauline exhortation, in Paul's own adjective-pair and Paul's vocative, given to a son named Lemuel in an Arabian valley. The 1830 spelling ('steadfast', 'immovable') has been modernized away from the KJV's 'stedfast, unmoveable' in every subsequent edition, so the first edition shows the borrowing more plainly than the current text does.

links.note: 'Firm, and steadfast, and immovable in keeping the commandments of the Lord' reproduces the adjective pair of 1 Corinthians 15:58, which is the KJV's only occurrence of the two words together and one of only two occurrences of 'unmoveable' at all. Paul's clause is an exhortation to brethren to hold fast in the Lord's work; Lehi's is an exhortation to a son to hold fast to the Lord's commandments. The phrase became one of the Book of Mormon's own formulae (Mosiah 5:15, Alma 1:25), which is how a borrowed phrase behaves once it has been absorbed.

pericopes.text: Now this he spake because of the stiffneckedness of Laman and Lemuel; for behold, they did murmur in many things against their father, because that he was a visionary man, and that he had led them out of the land of Jerusalem, to leave the land of their inheritance, and their gold, and their silver, and their precious things, and to perish in the wilderness. And this they said he had done because of the foolish imaginations of his heart.

links.text: And they said unto Moses, Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness? wherefore hast thou dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt?

provenance.route: The wilderness murmuring complaints → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.significance: The murmuring is not a character note; it is a citation. Israel's complaint has a fixed three-part shape — you brought us out, you took us from what we had, we shall die here — and Laman and Lemuel deliver all three parts in one verse. From this point the Book of Mormon can run the Exodus story with its own cast, and the reader knows which role each brother has been assigned by the way he complains.

links.note: 'They did murmur … because he had led them out of the land of Jerusalem, to leave the land of their inheritance … and to perish in the wilderness.' Every element is the Pentateuch's murmuring formula: the verb (Exodus 15:24, 16:2, 17:3, Numbers 14:2, all 'murmured against'), the charge that the leader brought them out (Exodus 14:11, Numbers 21:5), the loss of what they had, and death in the wilderness. Exodus 14:11 is the tightest single verse because it holds the accusation and the death-in-the-wilderness clause together, and because it too is spoken within sight of the Red Sea.

links.text: And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death; because he hath spoken to turn you away from the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed you out of the house of bondage, to thrust thee out of the way which the LORD thy God commanded thee to walk in. So shalt thou put the evil away from the midst of thee.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 13's law of the false dreamer → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'Visionary man' is not a KJV phrase at all, and the brothers' contempt needs no legal source; it may be nothing more than a son's word for a father who has ruined the family on the strength of a dream.
provenance.significance: If Deuteronomy 13 is in view, the brothers are not merely complaining — they are prosecuting. Deuteronomy 13:1-5 provides for exactly the case of a dreamer of dreams whose dream 'thrusts thee out of the way,' and prescribes death. That is the charge Laman and Lemuel bring, and in chapters 7 and 17 they twice attempt the sentence.

links.note: 'Because that he was a visionary man, and that he had led them out of the land of Jerusalem … and to perish in the wilderness.' The KJV has no 'visionary,' but it has a legal category for the offence being alleged: the 'dreamer of dreams' of Deuteronomy 13:1-5, who is to be put to death for speaking to 'thrust thee out of the way.' The brothers' complaint reproduces the statute's elements — dream, leading away, ruin — and their later conduct reproduces its penalty. Compare also Genesis 37:19, where elder brothers greet a younger visionary with 'Behold, this dreamer cometh,' and then plot his death.
links.whyNot: No shared wording, and the connection is made entirely by the reader supplying a statute the text never cites. A brother calling his father a dreamer is the most natural thing in the world and requires no Deuteronomic warrant. Kept because the accusation, the leading-away, and the two later murder attempts assemble the statute's whole structure, and because Genesis 37 shows the KJV already using that structure narratively.

pericopes.text: And thus Laman and Lemuel, being the eldest, did murmur against their father.— And they did murmur because they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them.

links.text: And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel.

provenance.alternative: 'Knew not God' is a commonplace of biblical indictment; 1 Samuel 2:12 says the same of Eli's sons.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:10 is the verse on which the whole book of Judges turns: a generation that did not know the LORD 'nor yet the works which he had done.' 1 Nephi 2:12 makes the same diagnosis of the same kind of failure — sons who did not know what God had done — and the Book of Mormon proceeds, like Judges, to run a cycle of apostasy and deliverance over it.

links.note: 'They did murmur because they knew not the dealings of that God who had created them.' The two KJV verses that state the fault this way are Judges 2:10 and 1 Samuel 2:12, and Judges 2:10 is the closer: not merely ignorance of God but ignorance of his *works*, which is exactly what 'dealings' names. The Book of Mormon's word is unusual — 'dealings' is what a chronicler says when he means the record of what God has done — and the sentence works as a thesis for the two brothers' whole arc.

pericopes.text: Neither did they believe that Jerusalem, that great city, could be destroyed according to the words of the prophets. And they were like unto the Jews, which were at Jerusalem, which sought to take away the life of my father.

links.text: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.

provenance.route: Jonah's 'that great city' → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV reads 'that great city' of Nineveh (Jonah 1:2, 3:2, 4:11) and of Babylon (Revelation 14:8, 16:19, 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21). It is applied to Jerusalem in exactly one verse, Revelation 11:8, and there as 'the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt.'
provenance.significance: The epithet the KJV reserves for Nineveh and Babylon is transferred to Jerusalem in the clause that denies Jerusalem can fall. Jonah's Nineveh is the case that proves the transfer apt: a great city warned by a prophet, whose destruction was announced in forty days and then withheld. Laman and Lemuel disbelieve on Jonah's premise and are wrong; the one KJV verse that does call Jerusalem 'the great city' calls it Sodom and Egypt in the same breath.

links.note: 'Neither did they believe that Jerusalem, that great city, could be destroyed according to the words of the prophets.' The demonstrative epithet is Jonah's for Nineveh and Revelation's for Babylon, and the sentence hands it to Jerusalem while reporting a refusal to believe the prophets — which is the situation of Jonah 3 with the response reversed, Nineveh having believed. Whether or not Jonah is the specific source, the epithet is not neutral in the KJV: every city that carries it is a city under sentence.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that my father did speak unto them in the valley of Lemuel, with power, being filled with the spirit, until their frames did shake before him. And he did confound them, that they durst not utter against him; wherefore they did do as he commanded them.

links.text: But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD, and of judgment, and of might, to declare unto Jacob his transgression, and to Israel his sin.

provenance.other: 'Full of power by the spirit' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The nearest New Testament analogues (Luke 4:14, 'in the power of the Spirit'; Acts 4:8, 'filled with the Holy Ghost, said unto them') separate the two nouns that Micah and 1 Nephi 2:14 join.
provenance.significance: Micah 3:8 is the prophet's self-authentication against the false prophets of 3:5-7, and its stated purpose is 'to declare unto Jacob his transgression.' That is precisely the office Lehi performs in 2:14 — he speaks against his sons with power and confounds them — one verse after they have accused him of being a false dreamer (2:11). The chapter stages the Micah 3 contest between true and false prophecy inside one family.

links.note: 'My father did speak unto them in the valley of Lemuel, with power, being filled with the spirit.' The KJV joins power and spirit in this way once: Micah 3:8. The context is the tighter half of the case. Micah's boast is made against prophets who prophesy falsely, and its object is the rebuke of his own people's transgression; Lehi's power is exercised against sons who have just called him a visionary, and its object is their rebuke. Compare the New Testament's version of the same authentication at Acts 4:8-13, where hearers likewise cannot answer.

links.text: And after that they durst not ask him any question at all.

provenance.route: The silencing of the questioners → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'Durst not' is simply the KJV's way of saying 'dared not', and a father silencing his sons needs no Gospel precedent.
provenance.significance: The Gospel scene is a formal one: a teacher answers hostile interrogators until they are confounded and stop asking. Luke and Matthew both close the temple controversies with it. 1 Nephi 2:14 closes the family controversy the same way, and the verb it uses to do so ('confound') is Acts 9:22's verb for what Paul does to the Damascus synagogue.

links.note: 'He did confound them, that they durst not utter against him.' 'Durst not' occurs in four KJV verses, and the one that describes the end of a public dispute is Luke 20:40, with Matthew 22:46 as its parallel — after the confounding, no one dares speak again. 'Confound' in that same sense is Acts 9:22, of Paul confounding the Jews at Damascus. Small verbal contact, but the two rare words arrive together and describe the same outcome.

pericopes.text: And my father dwelt in a tent.

And it came to pass that I, Nephi, being exceeding young, nevertheless being large in stature, and also having great desires to know of the mysteries of God, wherefore I did cry unto the Lord; and behold he did visit me, and did soften my heart that I did believe all the words which had been spoken by my father; wherefore I did not rebel against him like unto my brothers.

links.text: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.

provenance.other: 'Mysteries of God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'The mysteries of' occurs in three (Matthew 13:11 and Luke 8:10, both 'the mysteries of the kingdom').
provenance.significance: The phrase is Paul's name for what an apostle is entrusted with, not what a boy may ask for; the Gospels make it something 'given' to disciples and withheld from outsiders. Nephi's 'great desires to know of the mysteries of God' claims that access directly, by prayer, and gets it — which is the epistemology the whole book will run on and the specific claim his brothers deny in 15:8-11.

links.note: 'Having great desires to know of the mysteries of God' takes its object from 1 Corinthians 4:1, the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, where the mysteries of God are what stewards are trusted with. The Gospel form ('to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven', Matthew 13:11) supplies the verb. What follows in Nephi's verse is the answer to the request — 'he did visit me, and did soften my heart' — set deliberately against 'the hardness of their hearts' two verses later; compare Ezekiel 36:26 and Job 23:16, 'God maketh my heart soft.'

pericopes.text: And I spake unto Sam, making known unto him the things which the Lord had manifested unto me by his Holy Spirit. And it came to pass that he believed in my words;
but behold Laman and Lemuel would not hearken unto my words: And being grieved because of the hardness of their hearts, I cried unto the Lord for them.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: 'Hardness of their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and 'grieved … the hardness' in the same one. Mark 3:5 is the only place in the English Bible where the participle 'being grieved' governs that phrase.
provenance.significance: Recovering the context is what makes the borrowing say something. In Mark 3:5 the one who is grieved at hardness of heart is Jesus, in the synagogue, looking round on men who are watching to see whether he will heal on the sabbath so that they may accuse him. The clause puts Nephi in that position and his brothers in the position of the watchers — and the next thing Mark's Jesus does is heal, while the next thing Nephi does is pray for them. Neither text says this. The clause says it.

links.note: 'And being grieved because of the hardness of their hearts, I cried unto the Lord for them' against Mark 3:5's 'being grieved for the hardness of their hearts.' Seven words in sequence, with only the preposition altered, reproducing a participial clause from the one KJV verse in which that clause exists — 'hardness of their hearts' is unique to Mark 3:5 in the whole English Bible. This is the strongest verbal case in the chapter and the one link here that the n-gram stream found unaided. It falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his quotations; it is catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule that a reproduced clause from an identifiable single verse is one regardless of length.

links.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

provenance.other: 'Hearken unto my words' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 is the prophet-like-unto-Moses passage, which 1 Nephi 22:20 will quote outright and which the Book of Mormon treats as its own charter. Its sanction clause — whoever will not hearken unto my words shall be required of — is spoken here, in Nephi's own voice, about his brothers. The book's youngest son takes up the Mosaic prophet's formula in the second chapter of his record, twenty chapters before he cites the passage it comes from.

links.note: 'Laman and Lemuel would not hearken unto my words.' The phrase belongs to exactly one KJV verse, and it is not an incidental one: Deuteronomy 18:19 is the sanction attached to the promise of a prophet like unto Moses, the passage Nephi quotes at 1 Nephi 22:20 and argues from at 17:53-55. Nephi describes his brothers' refusal in the terms Deuteronomy uses for refusing that prophet, which is a claim about himself made by the choice of a phrase.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord spake unto me, saying: Blessed art thou, Nephi, because of thy faith, for thou hast sought me diligently, with lowliness of heart.

links.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

provenance.other: 'Diligently seek' occurs in two KJV verses (Proverbs 11:27, Hebrews 11:6).
provenance.significance: The Lord's commendation gives faith and diligent seeking as the two grounds of the blessing, and rewards them with a land; Hebrews 11:6 gives the same two as the conditions of pleasing God, and 11:8-9 gives the reward as a land of promise. Read together, 2:19-20 is Hebrews 11:6-9 in the order Hebrews has them.

links.note: 'Blessed art thou, Nephi, because of thy faith, for thou hast sought me diligently.' Hebrews 11:6 supplies both terms — faith, and God as 'a rewarder of them that diligently seek him' — and the very next clause of 1 Nephi 2 supplies the reward. The rest of the Hebrews 11 cluster is catalogued at 2:3, 2:4 and 2:20; this is the verse where the chapter names the criterion the chapter has been illustrating.

links.text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

provenance.other: 'Lowly in heart' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's variant 'lowliness of heart' is not a KJV phrase at all, though 'lowliness' appears at Ephesians 4:2 and Philippians 2:3.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:29 is Christ's self-description, offered as the condition of learning from him. 1 Nephi 2:19 makes it the condition of being taught by the Lord directly — Nephi is commended for approaching in the posture Christ names as his own.

links.note: 'With lowliness of heart' inverts the KJV's one occurrence of 'lowly in heart' (Matthew 11:29) into a noun phrase. The inversion is what keeps this at moderate rather than higher: an echo that changes the part of speech is harder to demonstrate than one that does not, and 'lowliness' was available to the writer from Ephesians 4:2 without Matthew. But 'lowly in heart' exists in one verse, and that verse is about the disposition in which one is taught by God, which is what 2:19 is rewarding.
links.whyNot: One rare phrase, and it has been grammatically recast. 'Lowliness' and 'heart' are both common enough that their combination could be independent, and the Pauline 'lowliness of mind' (Philippians 2:3) is closer in form to the Book of Mormon's genitive than Matthew's adjective is.

pericopes.text: And inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper, and shall be led to a land of promise; yea, even a land which I have prepared for you; yea, a land which is choice above all other lands.

links.text: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

provenance.other: 'Land of promise' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Old Testament never uses the phrase; it says 'the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee' and its variants. The English expression that the Book of Mormon uses more than any other for its own geography enters the English Bible at Hebrews 11:9 and nowhere else.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's most consequential finding for the project's thesis. A phrase the Book of Mormon treats as ordinary biblical vocabulary — the land of promise, from here to Ether — is not Old Testament vocabulary at all, and in the KJV belongs to a single New Testament verse about Abraham sojourning in tents. Recover that verse's context and the whole of 1 Nephi 2 is in it: called out by faith (2:3, 2:19), leaving an inheritance (2:4), dwelling in a tent (2:15), heir to a promise (2:20). Lehi's family is living in Hebrews 11:9, and saying so in Hebrews 11:9's words.

links.note: 'Ye shall prosper, and shall be led to a land of promise.' The phrase is unique in the KJV to Hebrews 11:9, and its one occurrence there is embedded in the exact scenario this chapter narrates: a man who left an inheritance at a call, sojourning as a stranger, dwelling in tents, holding a promise he does not yet possess. 1 Nephi 2:15 — 'And my father dwelt in a tent' — is the same verse's other half, and the phrase 'land of promise' then governs the Book of Mormon's self-description for a thousand years of its narrative. That an Old Testament family should describe its destination in the one phrase that exists only in the Epistle to the Hebrews is the sort of fact this catalogue is built to record.

links.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.route: The Deuteronomic prosperity conditional → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV joins commandment-keeping to prospering in three verses: Joshua 1:7, 1 Kings 2:3, and (of a different subject) 3 John 1:2. 1 Kings 2:3 and Joshua 1:7 are both deathbed or commissioning charges to a successor.
provenance.significance: The formula the Book of Mormon will repeat more than any other — keep the commandments and prosper in the land — is given here at its first appearance, and it arrives in the KJV's own diction from two verses that are both handovers of leadership: Moses to Joshua, David to Solomon. That is what 2:22 is about to make Nephi. The promise and the succession come in the same breath.

links.note: 'Inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments, ye shall prosper.' The conditional is Deuteronomic and the KJV's wording for it is 1 Kings 2:3 ('to keep his statutes, and his commandments … that thou mayest prosper') and Joshua 1:7 ('that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest'). Both are charges given to a man about to inherit a leadership, which is exactly the setting here: three verses later Nephi is made 'a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren.' The clause becomes the Book of Mormon's governing covenant formula.

links.text: In the day that I lifted up mine hand unto them, to bring them forth of the land of Egypt into a land that I had espied for them, flowing with milk and honey, which is the glory of all lands:

provenance.alternative: A superlative about a promised land is the most predictable thing such a promise could contain, and the Book of Mormon's word ('choice') is not Ezekiel's word ('glory').
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 20:6 is the KJV's one way of saying that the promised land outranks every other land, and Ezekiel says it inside an indictment: the land was given, and the generation that received it rebelled. 1 Nephi 2:20-24 does the same in four verses — the land is promised, and the rebellion is predicted before the promise is finished.

links.note: 'A land which is choice above all other lands' has no KJV phrase behind it, but it has a KJV idea with a fixed expression: 'the glory of all lands' (Ezekiel 20:6, 20:15), used twice of Canaan and nowhere else. Both Ezekiel verses are inside a rehearsal of Israel's rebellion in the wilderness, which is what 2:21-24 immediately turns to. Recorded as an echo, on sense and setting rather than on wording.

pericopes.text: And inasmuch as thy brethren shall rebel against thee, they shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord.

links.text: And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden.

provenance.other: 'From the presence of the LORD/Lord' occurs in eight KJV verses (Genesis 3:8, 4:16, Job 1:12, 2:7, Jonah 1:3, 1:10, Acts 3:19, 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Genesis 4:16 is the only one where the departure is a sentence passed on a brother; 2 Thessalonians 1:9 is the only one that makes it a punishment 'with everlasting destruction'.
provenance.significance: The Cain frame is the frame the rest of 1 Nephi will run on, and it is set here in a single clause. Elder brother resents the favoured younger, rebels, is cursed (2:23, 'I will curse them even with a sore curse'), is cut off from the presence of the LORD, and is nevertheless preserved with a mark and a limit on what may be done to him — 'they shall have no power over thy seed, except they shall rebel against me also' (2:23) is the Book of Mormon's version of Genesis 4:15. The prophecy of 2:21-24 is a compressed retelling of Genesis 4:11-16 with the sentence deferred to the seed.

links.note: 'They shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord.' The KJV's phrase for that exile is Genesis 4:16, where Cain goes out from the presence of the LORD after being cursed for what he did to his brother; the New Testament's is 2 Thessalonians 1:9, which supplies the eschatological weight the Book of Mormon's 'cut off' carries elsewhere. The Cain reading is preferred over the merely idiomatic one because verses 21-24 assemble the rest of Genesis 4 around it: rebellion against a favoured brother, a curse, a mark on the seed, and a divine restraint on how far the curse may go.

pericopes.text: And inasmuch as thou shalt keep my commandments, thou shalt be made a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren.

links.text: This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.

provenance.mt: Exodus 2:14 — 'Who made thee a man, a prince and a judge over us?'
provenance.route: Exodus 2:14 → Stephen's speech (Acts 7:27, 7:35) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV reads 'a prince and a judge' at Exodus 2:14 and 'a ruler and a judge' at Acts 7:27 and 7:35. The word 'ruler' in this formula exists only in the New Testament passages.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's mediation finding, and it is decisive because the two English forms differ in exactly the word the Book of Mormon uses. Had 1 Nephi 2:22 followed the Old Testament KJV it would read 'a prince'; it reads 'a ruler', which is Stephen's word, twice. Stephen's point in Acts 7:35 is that the very man the brethren refused as ruler was the one God sent as ruler and deliverer — and that is the whole plot of 1 Nephi: the brothers ask 'who made thee a ruler over us' at 16:37 and 18:10 while God confirms the appointment made here.

links.note: 'Thou shalt be made a ruler and a teacher over thy brethren' answers a KJV question that exists in two forms. Exodus 2:14 has the Hebrew challenge Moses in the sand: 'Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?' Acts 7:27 and 7:35 quote it as 'Who made thee a ruler and a judge?' The Book of Mormon takes the New Testament's noun, and it takes it into a promise rather than a challenge — and then hands the challenge back to Laman and Lemuel almost verbatim at 16:37 ('he thinketh to rule over us') and 17:44. Stephen's whole argument in Acts 7 is that the refused ruler is the sent one, and 1 Nephi is that argument in narrative.

pericopes.text: For behold, in that day that they shall rebel against me, I will curse them even with a sore curse, and they shall have no power over thy seed, except they shall rebel against me also.

links.text: Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest: because it is polluted, it shall destroy you, even with a sore destruction.

provenance.other: The construction 'even with a sore <noun>' occurs in two KJV verses: Deuteronomy 28:35 ('with a sore botch') and Micah 2:10 ('with a sore destruction').
provenance.significance: Micah 2:10 is a command to leave a polluted land before it destroys its inhabitants, which is the premise of the entire chapter — Lehi has been told to arise and depart from a Jerusalem under sentence. The verse the curse-formula comes from is the verse that would have authorized the journey.

links.note: 'I will curse them even with a sore curse' uses a KJV construction found in two verses, one of them Deuteronomy 28:35 in the covenant curses, the other Micah 2:10. Micah is the more interesting because of what its sentence says: 'Arise ye, and depart; for this is not your rest' — the departure command of 1 Nephi 2:2 — followed by destruction on those who stay. The formula and the situation come from the same verse.

pericopes.text: And if it so be that they rebel against me, they shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in the ways of remembrance.

links.text: Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations from before you; but they shall be snares and traps unto you, and scourges in your sides, and thorns in your eyes, until ye perish from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you.

provenance.other: 'Scourges in your sides' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The related figure — a people deliberately left in the land as 'pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides' — is Numbers 33:55 and Judges 2:3.
provenance.significance: Joshua 23:13 and Judges 2:21-3:4 give the Deuteronomistic doctrine of the useful enemy: nations left unconquered so that they may afflict Israel, and, in Judges' formulation, 'to prove Israel by them'. 1 Nephi 2:24 states the doctrine in one sentence and adds its own purpose clause — 'to stir them up in the ways of remembrance' — which is what the Judges cycle is for. The Lamanites are given their function in the book's second chapter, and it is Joshua's function for the Canaanites.

links.note: 'They shall be a scourge unto thy seed, to stir them up in the ways of remembrance.' The one KJV verse that makes a hostile people a scourge is Joshua 23:13, where nations are left in the land as 'scourges in your sides'; Judges 2:21-3:4 supplies the reason the Book of Mormon adds, that they remain 'to prove Israel by them.' Both source passages are about the consequences of not keeping the covenant, which is the condition 2:21-23 has just attached. The 1830 wording is unchanged here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I, Nephi, returned from speaking with the Lord, to the tent of my father.
And it came to pass that he spake unto me, saying: Behold I have dreamed a dream, in the which the Lord hath commanded me that thou and thy brethren shall return to Jerusalem.

links.text: And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.

provenance.other: 'I have dreamed a dream' occurs in three KJV verses: Genesis 37:9, Genesis 41:15 (Pharaoh), and Daniel 2:3 (Nebuchadnezzar). Only Genesis 37:9 is addressed by a family member to brethren.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the announcement is a provocation. Genesis 37:9 is the second dream, the one told to the brethren, and the sentence immediately following it in Genesis is 'and his brethren envied him.' 1 Nephi 3:2 puts the formula in Lehi's mouth and the next thing the chapter reports is that 'thy brothers murmur' (3:5). The Joseph frame is already running — 2:11 has them calling their father a visionary man — and the phrase that begins this chapter is the phrase that begins the enmity in Genesis.

links.note: 'Behold I have dreamed a dream' is a five-word run reproducing one of the KJV's three occurrences, and the choice among the three is settled by audience: Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar speak to their courts, Joseph speaks to his brothers. So does Lehi, and with the same result. 1 Nephi 8:2 opens the tree-of-life vision with the formula again ('Behold, I have dreamed a dream'), which is how a borrowed opening becomes a house style.

pericopes.text: For behold, Laban hath the record of the Jews, and also a genealogy of my forefathers, and they are engraven upon plates of brass.
Wherefore the Lord hath commanded me that thou and thy brothers should go unto the house of Laban, and seek the records, and bring them down hither into the wilderness.

links.text: Go unto the house of the Rechabites, and speak unto them, and bring them into the house of the LORD, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink.

provenance.alternative: 'Go unto the house of X' is an ordinary errand formula; the five shared words are four function words and a noun.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 35 is the chapter in which the Rechabites — a clan that dwells in tents, owns no field or vineyard, and keeps a father's commandment absolutely — are set before Judah as a rebuke, because they obeyed their father and Judah would not obey God. That is the whole moral machinery of 1 Nephi 3: a father's commandment, sons who obey or refuse, tents, and a renounced inheritance. If the errand formula came from Jeremiah 35:2, it came with the one chapter in the prophets that argues exactly what this chapter dramatizes.

links.note: 'Go unto the house of Laban, and seek the records.' The verbal contact with Jeremiah 35:2 is slight and would not be worth recording on its own. It is recorded because of what stands around it: Jeremiah 35 is the tent-dwelling, inheritance-refusing, father-obeying clan held up against a Jerusalem that will not listen — and 1 Nephi's Jeremiah frame is already established (1:4, 1:20, 2:1). Proposed as a deliberate risk under the generative posture; the case is thematic, and the wording is the occasion rather than the evidence.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, thy brothers murmur, saying: It is a hard thing which I have required of them; but behold I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord.

links.text: Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it?

provenance.other: 'An hard saying' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the very next verse supplies the reaction: 'When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it.' The pairing of a hard saying with murmuring exists in the English Bible only at John 6:60-61.
provenance.significance: John 6:60-66 is the passage where followers who cannot bear a commandment 'went back, and walked no more with him,' and where Jesus turns to the twelve and asks 'Will ye also go away?' 1 Nephi 3:5 sets the same test, and 3:14 reports the same near-defection: 'my brethren were about to return unto my father in the wilderness.' The Book of Mormon takes the Johannine crisis of discipleship and stages it as a family argument at the edge of Jerusalem.

links.note: 'Thy brothers murmur, saying: It is a hard thing which I have required of them.' Two elements arrive together and both are John 6's: the assessment of the command as hard, and the murmuring at it. 'An hard saying' exists in one KJV verse; the murmuring is in its neighbour. Lehi's rejoinder — 'behold I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord' — is the same correction Jesus makes in the next breath, that the offence is not the speaker's but the sender's.
