pericopes.text: Therefore go, my son, and thou shalt be favored of the Lord, because thou hast not murmured.

And it came to pass that I, Nephi, said unto my father, I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men, save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them.

links.text: And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.

provenance.route: Israel's covenant answer at Sinai → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'I will go and do' is not a KJV phrase; the resemblance is to the sense of the Sinai formula rather than its wording, and a willing answer to a divine errand could be modelled equally on Isaiah 6:8.
provenance.significance: The Sinai formula is spoken by a whole people and immediately broken by them; Nephi speaks it as an individual, alone among four brothers, and keeps it. The Book of Mormon's most quoted sentence is Israel's covenant answer with the plural taken out — which is the book's whole account of how a remnant works.

links.note: 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded' is the Book of Mormon's best known line and has no single KJV verse behind it. What it has is the Sinai answer — 'All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient' (Exodus 24:7; cf. 19:8, 24:3) — reduced from a nation's assent to one son's. Recorded as an allusion at moderate because the shape and function match exactly while no phrase is reproduced. The prophetic volunteer formula of Isaiah 6:8, 'Here am I; send me,' is the other available model and is noted rather than chosen; Nephi's line is a promise to perform, not an offer to be sent.

links.text: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

provenance.alternative: Paul's subject is temptation and Nephi's is commandment; the shared element is the general principle that God does not impose what he does not enable.
provenance.significance: Paul's guarantee is set inside a rehearsal of Israel's wilderness failures (1 Corinthians 10:1-11 — the cloud, the sea, the murmuring, 'neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured'), which is precisely the material 1 Nephi 2-3 is working with. Nephi answers his murmuring brothers with the doctrine Paul draws from murmuring Israel, in the chapter where Paul draws it.

links.note: 'The Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men, save he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them.' The logic and the structure are 1 Corinthians 10:13's — God will not impose beyond ability, but 'will with the temptation also make a way' — with 'way' doing the same work in both. The context strengthens it: Paul's guarantee comes at the end of a passage about Israel murmuring in the wilderness, and Nephi's is addressed to brothers who have just murmured.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when my father had heard these words, he was exceeding glad, for he knew that I had been blessed of the Lord.
And I, Nephi, and my brethren, took our journey in the wilderness with our tents, to go up to the land of Jerusalem.
And it came to pass that when we had come up to the land of Jerusalem, I and my brethren did consult one with another;

and we cast lots which of us should go in unto the house of Laban. And it came to pass that the lot fell upon Laman; and Laman went in unto the house of Laban, and he talked with him as he sat in his house.

links.text: And they said every one to his fellow, Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.

provenance.other: 'The lot fell upon' occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Jonah 1:7 and Acts 1:26 ('the lot fell upon Matthias').
provenance.significance: The two KJV lots do opposite work, and the chapter arguably wants both. Jonah's lot identifies the man on whose account disaster has come; Matthias's chooses a man for an apostolic errand. Laman's lot does the second and produces the first — he is chosen to go in, he fails, and Laban's enmity follows from his going. The Jonah frame is already open in this book (2:13, 'Jerusalem, that great city'), and Jonah is the prophet who runs from the errand, which is what Laman proposes at 3:14.

links.note: 'We cast lots which of us should go in unto the house of Laban … and the lot fell upon Laman.' Both the procedure and the result formula are KJV, and the result formula exists in only two verses. Nothing decides between them on wording alone, so both are kept — Jonah 1:7 as the source and Acts 1:26 as composite. Note what the casting of lots implies about the brothers at this point: an errand received by direct revelation is allocated by chance.

links.text: And the evil spirit from the LORD was upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his javelin in his hand: and David played with his hand.

provenance.other: 'As he sat in his house' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The phrase brings its scene with it, and the scene is the model for everything Laban does. 1 Samuel 19:9 is Saul seated at home with a javelin in his hand while the young man God has chosen plays before him; in the next verse he throws it. Laban sits in his house, receives the young men, and by verse 25 has sent servants to kill them. The Saul-and-David substructure then carries into chapter 4, where Nephi kills a drunken enemy with the man's own sword — which is 1 Samuel 17:51 exactly, and which David refuses to do to the sleeping Saul at 1 Samuel 26:8-11.

links.note: 'He talked with him as he sat in his house.' Six words reproducing the KJV's single occurrence, and the source verse is not incidental — it is the murderous-host scene of Saul with the javelin. From here the chapter is a Saul narrative: the great man in his house, the anger, the attempt on the young men's lives, the flight. The n-gram stream found this and ranked it below a Herod verse (see the exclusion at 3:8), which is the recall-floor problem in one page.

pericopes.text: And he desired of Laban the records which were engraven upon the plates of brass, which contained the genealogy of my father.

And behold, it came to pass that Laban was angry, and thrust him out from his presence; and he would not that he should have the records. Wherefore he said unto him, behold thou art a robber, and I will slay thee.
But Laman fled out of his presence, and told the things which Laban had done, unto us. And we began to be exceeding sorrowful, and my brethren were about to return unto my father in the wilderness.
But behold I said unto them, that as the Lord liveth, and as we live, we will not go down unto our father in the wilderness, until we have accomplished the thing which the Lord hath commanded us.

links.text: And Elijah said unto Elisha, Tarry here, I pray thee; for the LORD hath sent me to Bethel. And Elisha said unto him, As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee. So they went down to Bethel.

provenance.route: The doubled oath formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'As the LORD liveth, and as <someone> liveth' occurs in seven KJV verses. Four of them are 2 Kings 2:2, 2:4, 2:6 and 4:30, all Elisha refusing to turn back; the others are 1 Samuel 20:3, 1 Samuel 25:26 and 2 Samuel 15:21.
provenance.significance: The doubled oath is the KJV's formula for a refusal to abandon an errand, and its densest home is 2 Kings 2, where Elisha swears it three times in five verses against three invitations to stay behind. Nephi swears it once against his brothers' proposal to go back. Ittai's version (2 Samuel 15:21) is the other candidate and carries the same sense — 'whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be' — which is what 1 Nephi 3:15 is promising.

links.note: 'As the Lord liveth, and as we live, we will not go down unto our father in the wilderness, until we have accomplished the thing which the Lord hath commanded us.' Nephi does not use the simple oath ('as the LORD liveth', dozens of KJV verses) but the doubled one, which is rarer and which the KJV attaches specifically to refusals to turn back. Elisha's is the closest in function — three times refused permission to stop, three times the same oath — and 1 Nephi 3:15 is spoken against exactly that proposal. The only alteration is the plural: 'as thy soul liveth' becomes 'as we live', binding the brothers into an oath they did not swear.

pericopes.text: Wherefore let us be faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord; therefore let us go down to the land of our father’s inheritance, for behold he left gold and silver, and all manner of riches. And all this he hath done, because of the commandments of the Lord:
for he knowing that Jerusalem must be destroyed, because of the wickedness of the people.

links.text: The LORD shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me.

provenance.alternative: 'Because of the wickedness of' is a stock prophetic causal clause; Deuteronomy 9:4-5 uses it of the Canaanites and Jeremiah of Shiloh.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 28 is the covenant-curse chapter, and 28:20 states the mechanism the Book of Mormon will use for its entire national history: destruction follows wickedness, by covenant, and the destruction of Jerusalem is only its first instance. Nephi gives the reason for Jerusalem's fall in the vocabulary of the chapter that legislates it.

links.note: 'He knowing that Jerusalem must be destroyed, because of the wickedness of the people.' The pairing of destruction with 'because of the wickedness of' is Deuteronomy 28:20's, in the covenant curses, where destruction is the stipulated consequence rather than a misfortune. Note the 1830 participle: 'for he knowing that Jerusalem must be destroyed', corrected to 'knew' in 1920 — the first edition leaves the clause hanging in a way that reads as scriptural pastiche rather than as English.

pericopes.text: For behold, they have rejected the words of the prophets— Wherefore if my father should dwell in the land after that he hath been commanded to flee out of the land, behold he would also perish. Wherefore it must needs be that he flee out of the land.
And behold, it is wisdom in God that we should obtain these records, that we might preserve unto our children the language of our fathers;

and also that we may preserve unto them the words which have been spoken by the mouth of all the holy prophets, which have been delivered unto them by the spirit and power of God, since the world began, even down unto this present time.

links.text: Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.

provenance.other: 'By the mouth of all' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 3:18 and Acts 3:21, both in the same sermon. 'Since the world began' occurs in four (Luke 1:70, John 9:32, Acts 3:21, Romans 16:25). Acts 3:21 is the only verse in the English Bible that contains both.
provenance.significance: This is the most consequential single link in 1 Nephi 3, because of what else comes out of the same sermon. Peter's speech at Solomon's porch supplies 'the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began' here at 3:20; supplies Deuteronomy 18's prophet-like-unto-Moses at 1 Nephi 22:20, in Acts 3:22-23's wording rather than Deuteronomy's; and supplies Genesis 22:18's promise to Abraham's seed at 1 Nephi 15:18 and 22:9, in Acts 3:25's wording. Three of the four places 1 Nephi states its own theory of scripture and covenant come from one page of Acts. That is not an echo; it is a source.

links.note: 'The words which have been spoken by the mouth of all the holy prophets … since the world began.' Two phrases are reproduced, and both are rare: 'by the mouth of all' exists in two KJV verses and 'since the world began' in four, and exactly one verse — Acts 3:21 — has them together in this order with 'holy prophets' between them. Luke 1:70 is the near neighbour and shares three of the elements without 'all'. The passage falls below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his quotations; it is catalogued as a quotation because a whole clause of a single identifiable verse is reproduced with only the verb form altered. See the Acts 3 cluster noted under significance — this verse is where it starts.

links.text: And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Spirit and power of' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Gabriel's promise about John is that he will 'turn the hearts of the fathers to the children' — and the sentence borrowing his phrase is Nephi's argument for why records must be kept: 'that we might preserve unto our children the language of our fathers' (3:19). Fathers and children, in the verse before, and the phrase from the angel who joins them.

links.note: 'Delivered unto them by the spirit and power of God' takes a phrase the KJV uses once, of Elias. The transfer is minimal — 'of Elias' becomes 'of God' — and the sentence it lands in is already about fathers and children, which is Luke 1:17's own subject. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and the substitution generic; the same verse's neighbours (Acts 3:21) do the heavier work here.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after this manner of language did I persuade my brethren, that they might be faithful in keeping the commandments of God.
And it came to pass that we went down to the land of our inheritance, and we did gather together our gold, and our silver, and our precious things.
And after that we had gathered these things together, we went up again unto the house of Laban.

And it came to pass that we went in unto Laban, and desired him that he would give unto us the records which were engraven upon the plates of brass, for which we would give unto him our gold, and our silver, and all our precious things.

And it came to pass that when Laban saw our property, and that it was exceeding great, he did lust after it, insomuch that he thrust us out, and sent his servants to slay us, that he might obtain our property.

links.text: Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.

provenance.alternative: The sequence covet-then-kill is the tenth commandment's logic and needs no epistle; Ahab and Naboth (1 Kings 21) is the Old Testament's set-piece for it and is arguably the better narrative model.
provenance.significance: James 4:2 gives the anatomy of the sin in four verbs, in order — lust, have not, kill, obtain — and 1 Nephi 3:25 gives the same four in the same order in one sentence. What the New Testament states as a general diagnosis the Book of Mormon narrates as an event, which is what this book does with epistolary material throughout (compare the Pauline authentication formula at 1:3 and the Corinthian adjectives at 2:10).

links.note: 'When Laban saw our property, and that it was exceeding great, he did lust after it, insomuch that he thrust us out, and sent his servants to slay us, that he might obtain our property.' Set against James 4:2 the correspondence is sequential: lust · cannot have · kill · in order to obtain. No phrase is reproduced — 'lust after' is common KJV — so this is proposed on the shape of the sentence rather than its wording. The Ahab-and-Naboth alternative is recorded because 1 Kings 21 supplies a narrative that James is arguably already summarizing.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that we did flee before the servants of Laban, and we were obliged to leave behind our property, and it fell into the hands of Laban.
And it came to pass that we fled into the wilderness, and the servants of Laban did not overtake us, and we hid ourselves in the cavity of a rock.

links.text: When the men of Israel saw that they were in a strait, (for the people were distressed,) then the people did hide themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits.

provenance.route: The rock-refuge topos → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.alternative: 'The cavity of a rock' is not a KJV phrase at all — 'cavity' does not occur in the KJV — so no verbal case can be made, only a situational one.
provenance.significance: Two of the three candidates make hiding in rocks an eschatological image rather than a tactical one: Isaiah 2:10, 'Enter into the rock, and hide thee in the dust, for fear of the LORD', which Nephi transcribes at 2 Nephi 12:10; and Revelation 6:15, where the great and mighty hide 'in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains'. The men doing the hiding here are fleeing a mighty man who wanted to kill them for treasure, which inverts both.

links.note: 'We hid ourselves in the cavity of a rock.' The Book of Mormon's noun is not the KJV's, so this is recorded as an echo on situation only, and kept at moderate because the situation is a fixed biblical topos with three distinct settings — Saul's Israel hiding from the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:6), David in the cave of Adullam (22:1), and the eschatological hiding of Isaiah 2 and Revelation 6. The Saul narrative is preferred as the nearest neighbour because chapter 3 has been running on 1 Samuel since verse 11.
links.whyNot: No shared wording whatever; 'cavity' is not KJV vocabulary. Men fleeing armed pursuers hide among rocks in every literature, and the verse would read exactly as it does if no biblical passage lay behind it. Kept because the chapter's other links are already inside 1 Samuel, not because the sentence demands a source.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that Laman was angry with me, and also with my father; and also was Lemuel; for he hearkened unto the words of Laman. Wherefore Laman and Lemuel did speak many hard words unto us, their younger brothers, and they did smite us even with a rod.

links.text: And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab’s anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle.

provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 17 supplies the scene the whole chapter has been building toward and supplies it in the right order: the eldest brother's anger at the youngest for speaking (17:28), the objection that the enemy is too great and the youth too young (17:33), and the answer that the LORD will deliver him into my hand (17:46). 1 Nephi 3:28, 3:31 and 4:1-3 run the same three beats with the same speakers. The Book of Mormon then completes the type in chapter 4 by having the youth kill the armed man with the man's own sword and take his head (17:51).

links.note: 'Laman was angry with me, and also with my father … Wherefore Laman and Lemuel did speak many hard words unto us, their younger brothers.' Eliab's outburst is the KJV's one scene of an eldest brother's anger kindled against the youngest for zeal in a divine errand, and it stands immediately before the objection Laman makes three verses later, that the enemy is a mighty man. No wording is reproduced; the case rests on the sequence, which 1 Nephi 3-4 follows beat for beat and completes with the beheading.

links.text: And if a man smite his servant, or his maid, with a rod, and he die under his hand; he shall be surely punished.

provenance.alternative: The rod is the Bible's standard instrument of correction (Proverbs 23:13-14) and of tyranny (Isaiah 10:24), and a beating needs no statute behind it.
provenance.significance: Of the KJV's ten 'with a rod' verses, one describes a man striking a person in his own household: Exodus 21:20, the law of the beaten servant, whose point is that the victim is legally a person and the striker is punishable. The angel's intervention two verses later is that statute enforced — someone has been struck with a rod who was not a servant but a brother.

links.note: 'They did smite us even with a rod.' The KJV's rod is mostly a sceptre or a figure of judgment; the one verse where a man smites a member of his own household with one is Exodus 21:20, and its subject is precisely the status of the person struck. Read that way, the angel's question at 3:29 — 'why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod?' — is a charge under the statute, and the answer to it is the reversal of status the angel then announces.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass as they smote us with a rod, behold an angel of the Lord came and stood before them, and he spake unto them saying: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod? Know ye not that the Lord hath chosen him to be a ruler over you, and this because of your iniquities? Behold thou shalt go up to Jerusalem again, and the Lord will deliver Laban into your hands.

links.text: And the next day he shewed himself unto them as they strove, and would have set them at one again, saying, Sirs, ye are brethren; why do ye wrong one to another?

provenance.mt: Exodus 2:13-14 — 'Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? And he said, Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?'
provenance.route: Exodus 2:13-14 → Stephen's speech (Acts 7:26-27) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV has the intervention scene twice. Exodus 2:13-14: 'Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow?' … 'Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?' Acts 7:26-27: 'why do ye wrong one to another?' … 'Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?'
provenance.significance: This confirms the mediation call made at 1 Nephi 2:22, and confirms it by a second, independent element. Two things happen in 3:29 in a single speech: a third party interrupts men striking their brethren, and the striker is told that the struck man is to be a RULER over him. Those are Acts 7:26 and 7:27, consecutive verses, in order. The Old Testament original has the same two beats but says 'prince', and the Book of Mormon says 'ruler' at 2:22 and again here. Stephen's whole argument — that the brother refused as ruler is the one God sent (7:35) — is the argument the angel makes, and it is the argument 1 Nephi as a book exists to make.

links.note: 'Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod? Know ye not that the Lord hath chosen him to be a ruler over you?' The angel takes the role Moses takes in Exodus 2:13 and Stephen's Moses takes in Acts 7:26 — the intervener between striking brethren — and then states the very claim that Exodus 2:14 and Acts 7:27 put in the striker's mouth as a sneer. The Book of Mormon has answered the sneer in advance at 2:22, and here has an angel deliver the answer over a beating. The choice of 'ruler' rather than 'prince' identifies which of the two KJV versions is in play.

links.text: This day will the LORD deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel.

provenance.route: The holy-war delivery formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Deliver … into thine/mine hand' occurs in a dozen KJV verses, all of them sanctioning a killing or a conquest (Deuteronomy 7:24, Joshua 8:7, Judges 4:7, 7:7, 1 Samuel 17:46, 23:4, 24:4 and others).
provenance.significance: The formula is what makes chapter 4 possible. Every KJV occurrence licenses a killing in advance, and 1 Samuel 17:46 — the only one spoken by a youth about a mighty man, and the only one that goes on to name decapitation as the method — is the one whose narrative 1 Nephi 4 then carries out. The Spirit's argument to Nephi at 4:12-13 is a defence of a killing the angel has already authorized here, in the Bible's own language for authorizing killings.

links.note: 'Behold thou shalt go up to Jerusalem again, and the Lord will deliver Laban into your hands.' The clause is the Deuteronomistic holy-war formula, and the version standing closest is 1 Samuel 17:46, David's answer to Goliath, because it alone is spoken by the youngest brother against a mighty man and alone specifies the head. Chapter 4 supplies the head. Note the 1830 reading 'Behold thou shalt go up' where 1920 has 'ye shall' — the first edition addresses the command to one of the four, which reads as the angel singling Nephi out.

pericopes.text: And after that the angel had spoken unto us, he departed.

And after that the angel had departed, Laman and Lemuel again began to murmur, saying, how is it possible that the Lord will deliver Laban into our hands? Behold he is a mighty man, and he can command fifty, yea, even he can slay fifty; then why not us?

links.text: And Saul said to David, Thou art not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him: for thou art but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.

provenance.alternative: 'He is a mighty man' is a stock KJV description (2 Samuel 17:10 of David himself, and a dozen others), and the objection that an enemy is too strong is the oldest speech in war literature.
provenance.significance: The objection and the answer are both 1 Samuel 17's. Saul weighs the youth against the man of war; David answers by naming the LORD, and by arithmetic — the lion and the bear, and now this Philistine. Nephi answers his brothers the same way at 4:1, and answers with arithmetic too: 'the Lord is mightier than all the earth, then why not mightier than Laban and his fifty, yea, or even than his tens of thousands?' The number in that reply is 1 Samuel 18:7's, the women's song of Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands.

links.note: 'How is it possible that the Lord will deliver Laban into our hands? Behold he is a mighty man, and he can command fifty, yea, even he can slay fifty; then why not us?' This is Saul's objection at 1 Samuel 17:33 — the enemy's proven capacity against the youth's — put in the mouths of the elder brothers, three verses after the eldest-brother's anger of 17:28 was put there too. Recorded at high confidence on sequence: the Book of Mormon takes 1 Samuel 17's speeches in 1 Samuel 17's order and redistributes them among its own cast.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I spake unto my brethren, saying: Let us go up again unto Jerusalem, and let us be faithful in keeping the commandments of the Lord; for behold he is mightier than all the earth, then why not mightier than Laban and his fifty, yea, or even than his tens of thousands.

links.text: Then the king sent unto him a captain of fifty with his fifty. And he went up to him: and, behold, he sat on the top of an hill. And he spake unto him, Thou man of God, the king hath said, Come down.

provenance.other: 'With his fifty' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 2 Kings 1:9, 1:11 and 1:13, all of the same episode. Fifty as a unit commanded by one man is otherwise only the 'rulers of fifties' of Exodus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 1:15.
provenance.significance: Laman's objection at 3:31 was that Laban 'can command fifty, yea, even he can slay fifty'. The KJV's one story about a captain of fifty with his fifty is the story of two such companies consumed by fire at a prophet's word, and a third spared when its captain begs. So the arithmetic Nephi is answering has already been answered in scripture, and answered against the captain. Whether the writer intended the allusion or not, the number is not a neutral choice: in the KJV, fifty men under a commander are what a prophet destroys.

links.note: 'Why not mightier than Laban and his fifty, yea, or even than his tens of thousands.' The unit is named twice in two verses (3:31, 4:1) and the KJV has exactly one narrative for it: Elijah on the hill and the captains of fifty sent to fetch him. 'Tens of thousands' then reaches for the other half of the reply, the women's song of 1 Samuel 18:7 — Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands — which is the arithmetic of the David narrative the chapter has been running since 3:28.

pericopes.text: Therefore let us go up; let us be strong like unto Moses: For he truly spake unto the waters of the Red Sea, and they divided hither and thither, and our fathers came through out of captivity on dry ground, and the armies of Pharaoh did follow and were drowned in the waters of the Red Sea.

links.text: By faith they passed through the Red sea as by dry land: which the Egyptians assaying to do were drowned.

provenance.other: 'Drowned' occurs in five KJV verses; two are relevant here, Exodus 15:4 ('his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea') and Hebrews 11:29. Hebrews 11:29 is the only verse in the Bible that holds the Red Sea, the dry land, the Egyptians and the drowning in one sentence.
provenance.significance: This is the second stop on a route already established. 1 Nephi 2 built its departure out of Hebrews 11:8-9 — the call, the abandoned inheritance, the tent, the land of promise; 1 Nephi 4 builds its exhortation out of Hebrews 11:29, four verses further down the same chapter. The Book of Mormon is not merely echoing Hebrews 11; it is working through it in order, and using it as an index to the Old Testament episodes it wants.

links.note: 'For he truly spake unto the waters of the Red Sea, and they divided hither and thither, and our fathers came through out of captivity on dry ground, and the armies of Pharaoh did follow and were drowned in the waters of the Red Sea.' Every element of Hebrews 11:29 is here in Hebrews' order: passage through the Red Sea, dry land, the Egyptians following, the drowning. Exodus supplies the narrative but not this compression — Exodus 14 takes nine verses to say it and never uses 'drowned', which is Exodus 15:4's word and Hebrews 11:29's. What Nephi is doing rhetorically is what Hebrews 11 does: reciting a past deliverance as a warrant for present courage.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 4.2 (Exodus 14:21-29, for the Red Sea crossing)

links.text: And Elijah took his mantle, and wrapped it together, and smote the waters, and they were divided hither and thither, so that they two went over on dry ground.

provenance.other: 'Hither and thither' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 2:8 and 2:14 — Elijah dividing the Jordan and Elisha dividing it after him. Exodus never uses the phrase: at 14:21 'the waters were divided', at 14:22 'the waters were a wall unto them'.
provenance.significance: Nephi attributes to Moses at the Red Sea a phrase that in the King James Bible belongs to Elijah and Elisha at the Jordan, and pairs it with 'on dry ground', which is 2 Kings 2:8's phrase as well as Joshua's. This is exactly the kind of finding the catalogue exists for: the sentence is presented as a recital of Exodus and is worded out of 2 Kings. Note that chapter 3 has already drawn on the same page of 2 Kings — Elisha's doubled oath at 2:2 stands behind 1 Nephi 3:15 — so the Book of Mormon's Moses is being described in Elijah's and Elisha's borrowed language, six verses apart in the source.

links.note: 'He truly spake unto the waters of the Red Sea, and they divided hither and thither … on dry ground.' The two distinctive phrases in the clause are 2 Kings 2:8's, and 2 Kings 2:8 is not about Moses or the Red Sea. Its subject is the prophet whose mantle passes to a successor who then repeats the miracle — which is what 1 Nephi 4:2 is asking for when it says 'let us be strong like unto Moses'. The Book of Mormon wants the succession, and it has reached for the succession passage's words.

pericopes.text: Now behold ye know that this is true; and ye also know that an angel hath spoken unto you, wherefore can ye doubt. Let us go up; the Lord is able to deliver us, even as our fathers, and to destroy Laban, even as the Egyptians.

links.text: If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.

provenance.alternative: 'Able to deliver' is ordinary confession-language (2 Chronicles 32:14, Isaiah 36:14-20 in Rabshakeh's mouth); the five-word run may be generic.
provenance.significance: Daniel 3:17 is a confession made by young men of Judah, in exile, to the face of a power that intends to kill them — and made without a guarantee ('but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods'). Nephi is arguing his brothers into a house where a man has already tried to have them killed, and the sentence he uses is the one three brothers-in-faith used in Babylon.

links.note: 'The Lord is able to deliver us, even as our fathers, and to destroy Laban, even as the Egyptians.' The confession formula is Daniel 3:17's, and the situation matches at every point that matters: young Judahites, a lethal adversary, a statement of God's ability rather than a prediction of his action. The second half of the sentence returns to Hebrews 11:29's Egyptians, so the verse joins the Red Sea recital of 4:2 to the courage formula of Daniel 3.

pericopes.text: Now when I had spoken these words, they were yet wroth, and did still continue to murmur; Nevertheless they did follow me up until we came without the walls of Jerusalem.
And it was by night; and I caused that they should hide themselves without the walls. And after that they had hid themselves, I, Nephi, crept into the city and went forth towards the house of Laban.
And I was led by the spirit, not knowing beforehand the things which I should do.

links.text: By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.

provenance.other: 'Led by the Spirit' is Luke 4:1 (into the wilderness), Romans 8:14 and Galatians 5:18. The 'not knowing' clause is Hebrews 11:8's.
provenance.significance: One short verse holds both halves of the chapter's inheritance from Hebrews 11. The obedience clause of 11:8 was used at 2:3 for Lehi's departure; its second half — 'not knowing whither he went' — is used here for Nephi's entry into the city. And the phrase that carries it, 'led by the Spirit', is Luke's for Jesus going into the wilderness to be tempted, which is what Nephi is walking into: a test he will fail twice before obeying.

links.note: 'And I was led by the spirit, not knowing beforehand the things which I should do.' Two New Testament phrases in one sentence, and the second is Hebrews 11:8's clause about Abraham with 'whither he went' changed to 'the things which I should do' — a change that matters, because what Nephi does not know in advance is not a destination but an act. The verse is the hinge of the chapter: it establishes in advance that the killing was not premeditated, and it does so in the words the New Testament uses for faith that moves without information.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless I went forth, and as I came near unto the house of Laban, I beheld a man, and he had fallen to the earth before me, for he was drunken with wine.
And when I came to him, I found that it was Laban.

And I beheld his sword, and I drew it forth from the sheath thereof, and the hilt thereof was of pure gold, and the workmanship thereof was exceeding fine; and I saw that the blade thereof was of the most precious steel.

links.text: Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.

provenance.other: Eight KJV verses contain 'sheath'; only 1 Samuel 17:51 has a man drawing another man's sword out of the sheath thereof in order to behead him with it.
provenance.significance: This is where the chain begun at 3:28 closes. 1 Samuel 17 has supplied the elder brother's anger (17:28), the objection that the enemy is a mighty man (17:33), and the promise that the LORD will deliver him into my hand and I will take his head (17:46). Now it supplies the act, in the order the source has it: take his sword · draw it out of the sheath thereof · slay him · cut off his head therewith. 1 Nephi splits the sequence across two verses, 4:9 and 4:18, with the moral crisis inserted between them — which is the Book of Mormon's one addition to the type, and the only part of it that is not David's.

links.note: 'And I beheld his sword, and I drew it forth from the sheath thereof.' The phrase 'the sheath thereof' occurs in the KJV in one narrative of a killing, and that narrative continues 'and slew him, and cut off his head therewith' — which is 1 Nephi 4:18. Nine verses of hesitation stand between the drawing and the stroke, and they are the Book of Mormon's own; the frame around them is 1 Samuel 17:51 taken apart and put back together. The description of the workmanship (gold hilt, precious steel) has no KJV source and reads as the writer furnishing what the type does not supply.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I was constrained by the spirit that I should kill Laban; but I said in my heart, never at any time have I shed the blood of man, and I shrunk and would that I might not slay him.

links.text: Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

provenance.alternative: 'Shed blood' is one of the KJV's commonest legal collocations; Nephi's objection may be simple revulsion rather than a citation.
provenance.significance: Genesis 9:6 is the Bible's foundational homicide statute, given to Noah, grounding the prohibition in the image of God rather than in covenant law — which makes it the one prohibition that binds a pre-Sinai and non-Israelite world, and therefore the one Nephi cannot answer by appeal to the law of Moses he is about to go and fetch. His justification at 4:13 has to come from somewhere else, and it comes from Caiaphas.

links.note: 'Never at any time have I shed the blood of man, and I shrunk and would that I might not slay him.' The objection is stated in the vocabulary of Genesis 9:6, the shedding of man's blood, which is the statute rather than the sixth commandment's 'thou shalt not kill' — a distinction that matters, since Genesis 9:6 makes the killing of a man an offence against the divine image and requires the killer's own blood in return. The verse is the strongest possible form of the objection Nephi is about to override.

pericopes.text: And the spirit saith unto me again, behold the Lord hath delivered him into thy hands; yea, and I also knew that he had sought to take away mine own life; yea, and he would not hearken unto the commandments of the Lord; and he also had taken away our property.

links.text: And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the LORD said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee. Then David arose, and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe privily.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 24 and 26 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The 'delivered into thine hand' formula is common; what is not common is the scene it is used for here. Twice in 1 Samuel a helpless enemy is found by David, twice a companion tells him God has delivered the enemy into his hand, and twice David refuses to strike.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon puts its hero in David's exact position and has him do the opposite, and this is the single most important interpretive fact about 1 Nephi 4. Laban is drunk as Saul is asleep (1 Samuel 26:12, 'a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them'); a voice at Nephi's side says what Abishai says — 'God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day: now therefore let me smite him' (26:8); Nephi shrinks as David refuses. Then the voice speaks again, and Nephi kills. Whatever else 1 Nephi 4 is doing, it is answering 1 Samuel 24 and 26 — and the answering voice has to be identified as the Spirit precisely because the scriptural precedent runs the other way.

links.note: 'The spirit saith unto me again, behold the Lord hath delivered him into thy hands.' The words are the KJV's holy-war formula, but the scene is specifically 1 Samuel 24:4 and 26:8: an enemy incapacitated, a companion urging that God has handed him over, and the question whether providence licenses the stroke. David's answer is no, twice, and the narrative counts that refusal as his righteousness. Nephi's is yes, and the chapter spends verses 10-18 arguing for it — the hesitation, the reasons, the appeal to a nation's future. The 1830 present tense, 'the spirit saith unto me', puts the reader inside the deliberation rather than after it; 1920 changed it to 'said'.

links.text: And they were to prove Israel by them, to know whether they would hearken unto the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.

provenance.alternative: 'Hearken unto the commandments of the LORD' is a Deuteronomic formula and appears at Deuteronomy 28:13 in the same seven words.
provenance.significance: Judges 3:4 is the verse the catalogue has already met at 1 Nephi 2:24, where the nations left in the land are 'to prove Israel by them'. Laban is now charged under the same standard the Lamanites will be used to enforce — he 'would not hearken unto the commandments of the Lord', which is the test the verse defines. The indictment and the sentence come from one place.

links.note: A seven-word run shared with Judges 3:4 and Deuteronomy 28:13. Judges 3:4 is preferred because 1 Nephi 2:24 has already drawn on its immediate context — the nations left to prove Israel — so the formula arrives with a history in this book. Its function at 4:11 is legal: the second of three grounds Nephi lists for the killing, between the attempt on his life and the theft of the property.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the spirit said unto me again, slay him, for the Lord hath delivered him into thy hands.
Behold the Lord slayeth the wicked to bring forth his righteous purposes: It is better that one man should perish, than that a nation should dwindle and perish in unbelief.

links.text: Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.

provenance.other: 'One man should die' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 11:50 and John 18:14, which is John repeating the same saying. No Old Testament verse states the calculus.
provenance.significance: This is the most loaded borrowing in 1 Nephi, and its force is entirely metaleptic. The sentence Nephi uses to justify killing Laban is the sentence Caiaphas uses to justify killing Jesus — and John, in the very next verse, says Caiaphas 'spake not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied.' So the formula arrives already marked in its source as both a cynical expedient and an unwitting truth. Whoever put it in Nephi's mouth put both readings there with it: either the killing of Laban is a small atonement that saves a nation, or it is what a high priest says when he has decided to kill someone. The catalogue does not have to choose; recording the borrowing is what makes the choice visible.

links.note: 'It is better that one man should perish, than that a nation should dwindle and perish in unbelief.' Against John 11:50: 'it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.' The proposition, the arithmetic, the two nouns and the comparative structure are all reproduced; only 'expedient' becomes 'better' and 'the people' becomes the reason for the loss, unbelief. The saying exists in the KJV in two verses and both are John reporting Caiaphas. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

pericopes.text: And now, when I, Nephi, had heard these words, I remembered the words of the Lord which he spake unto me in the wilderness, saying, that inasmuch as thy seed shall keep my commandments, they shall prosper in the land of promise.—

links.text: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:

provenance.other: 'Land of promise' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. See the full argument at 1 Nephi 2:20.
provenance.significance: The first clean case in the corpus of a Book of Mormon verse whose proximate model is an earlier Book of Mormon verse rather than the Bible. 4:14 says so itself — 'I remembered the words of the Lord which he spake unto me in the wilderness' — and then quotes 2:20 with one change, from 'ye shall prosper' to 'thy seed shall keep my commandments, they shall prosper', which extends the promise a generation. The biblical phrase is reaching this verse through the book's own earlier text, and the catalogue should say so rather than record a second independent hit on Hebrews 11:9.
provenance.alternative: Read as a direct borrowing, 4:14 is simply the same Hebrews 11:9 link again; nothing in the wording forbids that. What decides it is the verse's own claim to be a recollection.

links.note: Nephi quotes the promise of 2:20 back to himself while standing over a corpse, and the quotation is the argument: obtaining the law is what makes the land-promise keepable, so the killing serves the covenant. Catalogued with mediation 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' because the proximate model is 1 Nephi 2:20. **Schema note for Wilson:** the enum value says OT, and the ultimate source here is a New Testament verse. The category is right and its name is not; it wants to be 'via-earlier-BoM'. Flagged rather than fudged (CONVENTIONS preamble).

pericopes.text: Yea, and I also thought that they could not keep the commandments of the Lord according to the law of Moses, save they should have the law.
And I also knew that the law was engraven upon the plates of brass.

links.text: Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.

provenance.alternative: The premise that a law must be possessed to be kept is self-evident and needs no source; and the Josianic reform is a generation before Lehi in the narrative, not a text he would cite.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's whole plot device — a written law recovered out of Jerusalem, and a people who cannot keep what they do not have — is the plot of 2 Kings 22. Hilkiah finds the book, Josiah tears his clothes because 'our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book', the law is read aloud, and a reform follows. 1 Nephi 3-5 runs the same sequence with the recovery moved outside the city: the plates are fetched at the cost of a life, and Lehi reads them at 5:10. The difference is the direction of travel. Josiah's book stays in Jerusalem and does not save it; Lehi's leaves.

links.note: 'And I also knew that the law was engraven upon the plates of brass' — with 4:15, 'they could not keep the commandments of the Lord according to the law of Moses, save they should have the law.' Proposed on the situation rather than on wording: a Judahite book of the law recovered, and a people's obedience made to depend on possessing it. 2 Kings 22:13's 'our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book' is also the verse the machine stream reached at 1 Nephi 3:28, which is where the brothers refuse the errand.

pericopes.text: And again—I knew that the Lord had delivered Laban into my hands, for this cause: that I might obtain the records according to his commmandments.
Therefore I did obey the voice of the spirit, and took Laban by the hair of the head, and I smote off his head with his own sword.

links.text: Therefore David ran, and stood upon the Philistine, and took his sword, and drew it out of the sheath thereof, and slew him, and cut off his head therewith. And when the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.

provenance.other: Three KJV verses describe striking off a head: Judges 5:26 (Jael and Sisera), 1 Samuel 17:51 (David and Goliath), 1 Samuel 31:9 (the Philistines and Saul). Only 1 Samuel 17:51 does it with the dead man's own sword drawn from his own sheath. 'The hair of the head' is Numbers 6:18's phrase, from the Nazarite law, and is the one detail with no source in the David narrative.
provenance.significance: The killing is narrated in the words of Israel's founding single combat, and the effect is to make Laban a Goliath — an armed champion, in armour, who threatened the covenant people and whose own weapon undoes him. But the sequence 1 Nephi has actually run is 1 Samuel 24 and 26 (see 4:11), where the same David spares a helpless enemy. The chapter borrows its act from 17:51 and its situation from 24:4, and the two do not agree. That disagreement is the chapter's whole moral problem, and it is legible only when both borrowings are catalogued.

links.note: 'I took Laban by the hair of the head, and I smote off his head with his own sword.' The second half of 1 Samuel 17:51, whose first half was used at 4:9: the sword taken, drawn out of the sheath thereof, and the head cut off therewith. The Book of Mormon adds the hair — the KJV's one 'hair of the head' is Numbers 6:18, the Nazarite's — and adds nothing else. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because the clause and its sequence are reproduced from one identifiable verse.

pericopes.text: And after that I had smitten off his head with his own sword, I took the garments of Laban and put them upon mine own body; yea, even every whit; and I did gird on his armour about my loins.

links.text: And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David, and his garments, even to his sword, and to his bow, and to his girdle.

provenance.other: The KJV's transfer-of-arms scene comes in two forms in the same narrative: Saul putting his armour on David, which David takes off because he has not proved it (17:38-39), and Jonathan giving David his robe, his garments, his sword and his girdle (18:4).
provenance.significance: The items match Jonathan's list — garments, sword, girdle — and the inversion is total. Jonathan strips himself and gives; Nephi strips a corpse and takes. Jonathan's gift makes David his brother by covenant in the verse before (18:3); Nephi's theft makes him another man entirely, and the next thing he does with the identity is deceive a servant. The chapter has been drawing on 1 Samuel for two chapters, and this is the point where it turns the source inside out.

links.note: 'I took the garments of Laban and put them upon mine own body; yea, even every whit; and I did gird on his armour about my loins.' The list is 1 Samuel 18:4's — garments, and the girding on of a sword — and the sequence is 1 Samuel 17-18's, where the armour scene follows the beheading. Note 'every whit', which is not a KJV item-list phrase but a KJV totality phrase (John 7:23, 13:10), doing the work of Jonathan's 'even to his … and to his … and to his'. The 1830 'girted about my loins' at 4:21 was corrected to 'girded' in 1920.

pericopes.text: And after that I had done this, I went forth unto the treasury of Laban. And as I went forth towards the treasury of Laban, behold I saw the servant of Laban which had the keys of the treasury. And I commanded him in the voice of Laban, that he should go with me into the treasury;
and he supposed me to be his master, Laban, for he beheld the garments, and also the sword girted about my loins.

links.text: And he discerned him not, because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esau’s hands: so he blessed him.

provenance.significance: Genesis 27 is the Bible's one sustained impersonation-by-garment scene, and every element of it is in 1 Nephi 4:20-26. Rebekah puts Esau's raiment on Jacob (27:15); Jacob says 'I am Esau thy firstborn' (27:19); Isaac cannot tell by the voice — 'the voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau' (27:22) — and 'discerned him not' (27:23). Nephi wears Laban's garments, speaks 'in the voice of Laban', and the servant 'supposed me to be his master'. The Book of Mormon has inverted the sensory test: Isaac is deceived by touch despite the voice, Zoram by the voice and the clothes together. And the point of both scenes is the same — a younger man takes what belongs to the elder by wearing his clothes.

links.note: 'He supposed me to be his master, Laban, for he beheld the garments, and also the sword girted about my loins … And I spake unto him as if it had been Laban.' No wording is reproduced; the case is the scene, which the KJV has only once. That it is the Jacob scene matters for this book in particular: 1 Nephi is a younger-brother narrative from its first chapter, its opening dream formula is Joseph's (3:2), and here its narrator obtains the family's records by putting on an older man's clothes and answering to his name.

pericopes.text: And he spake unto me concerning the elders of the Jews, he knowing that his master Laban had been out by night among them.
And I spake unto him as if it had been Laban.
And I also spake unto him that I should carry the engravings which were upon the plates of brass, to my elder brethren, which were without the walls.
And I also bade him that he should follow me.
And he, supposing that I spake of the brethren of the church, and that I was truly that Laban whom I had slain, wherefore he did follow me.
And he spake unto me many times concerning the elders of the Jews, as I went forth unto my brethren, which were without the walls.

And it came to pass that when Laman saw me, he was exceedingly frightened, and also Lemuel and Sam. And they fled from before my presence; for they supposed it was Laban, and that he had slain me, and had sought to take away their lives also.

links.text: And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live? And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence.

provenance.alternative: Men fleeing from what they take to be an enemy, and stopping when they recognize a voice, needs no source; and 'troubled at his presence' is not reproduced.
provenance.significance: The Joseph cycle has been running since 3:2 and this is its recognition scene. In Genesis the brothers do not know Joseph because he is dressed as an Egyptian and speaks through an interpreter; here they do not know Nephi because he is dressed as Laban and has been speaking in Laban's voice. Both scenes turn on the brother's own voice — 'Come near to me, I pray you' — and both end with terrified brothers approaching a younger brother who has power over them and does not use it.

links.note: 'They fled from before my presence; for they supposed it was Laban … And it came to pass that I called after them, and they did hear me; wherefore they did cease to flee from my presence.' The sequence is Genesis 45:3-4's: brothers unable to face a man they do not recognize, and a voice calling them back. Proposed on the shape rather than the wording; the chapter's disguise material is already Genesis 27's, and this is the other Genesis scene about brothers failing to recognize one of their own.
links.whyNot: The verbal contact is limited to 'presence', which the Book of Mormon uses twice here for its own reasons. Genesis 45 has a revelation of identity and 1 Nephi 4 has none — Nephi never says who he is, the brothers simply hear him. A reader could decline this and lose nothing but a resonance.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I called after them, and they did hear me; wherefore they did cease to flee from my presence.
And it came to pass that when the servant of Laban beheld my brethren, he began to tremble, and was about to flee from before me and return to the city of Jerusalem.
And now I, Nephi, being a man large in stature, and also having received much strength of the Lord, therefore I did seize upon the servant of Laban, and held him, that he should not flee.
And It came to pass that I spake with him, that if he would hearken unto my words, as the Lord liveth and as I live, even so that if he would hearken unto our words, we would spare his life.

links.text: And Elijah said unto Elisha, Tarry here, I pray thee; for the LORD hath sent me to Bethel. And Elisha said unto him, As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee. So they went down to Bethel.

provenance.route: The doubled oath formula → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: See the full argument at 1 Nephi 3:15. Seven KJV verses have 'as the LORD liveth, and as <someone> liveth'; four are Elisha's refusals to turn back.
provenance.significance: The same oath at both ends of the errand. At 3:15 Nephi swears it to bind his brothers to the task; at 4:32 he swears it to bind himself to sparing a man's life, seventeen verses after taking one. The formula is the chapter's measure of what an oath is worth, and the narrative makes the point explicitly at 4:37: once Zoram has sworn, 'our fears did cease concerning him.'

links.note: 'As the Lord liveth and as I live … we would spare his life.' The doubled oath again, in the singular this time. Recorded briefly; the argument for the formula is at 3:15 and is not repeated here. What is worth noting is the reciprocity — Nephi swears, Zoram swears back (4:35), and the second oath is what ends the scene.

links.text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.

provenance.other: 'Hearken unto my words' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Third occurrence of the phrase in four chapters, and the pattern is consistent: Nephi uses the sanction-clause of the prophet-like-unto-Moses passage for himself. At 2:18 his brothers would not hearken unto his words; here a servant is offered his life on condition that he will. Deuteronomy 18:19 promises that the one who refuses will be 'required of'; Zoram does not refuse.

links.note: 'If he would hearken unto my words … we would spare his life.' The unique KJV phrase again (see 2:18). Its recurrence is the argument: a formula reserved in the Old Testament for the prophet God will raise up is used by Nephi three times in four chapters about his own words, and 1 Nephi 22:20 will quote the passage it comes from outright.

pericopes.text: And I spake unto him, even with an oath, that he need not fear; that he should be a free man like unto us, if he would go down in the wilderness with us.

links.text: For he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord’s freeman: likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ’s servant.

provenance.alternative: 'Free man' is ordinary English and the offer of manumission needs no epistolary source; Deuteronomy 15:12-15 legislates the freeing of a Hebrew servant and is the obvious Old Testament candidate.
provenance.significance: 'Freeman' is a rare KJV word — two verses — and one of them is Paul's paradox that a servant called in the Lord is already the Lord's freeman. That is exactly the transaction of 4:32-35: Laban's servant is offered freedom on the condition that he bind himself by oath to another master's errand. Zoram gains liberty by swearing service, which is 1 Corinthians 7:22 in narrative.

links.note: 'That he should be a free man like unto us, if he would go down in the wilderness with us.' The KJV has 'freeman' twice, and only 1 Corinthians 7:22 gives the word a doctrine. Recorded as an echo because nothing is reproduced beyond the term itself, and because Deuteronomy 15's manumission law is a live alternative — but Deuteronomy releases a servant at the seventh year and Paul makes freedom and service the same thing, which is the shape Zoram's oath actually takes.

pericopes.text: And I also spake unto him, saying, surely the Lord hath commanded us to do this thing. And shall we not be diligent in keeping the commandments of the Lord? Therefore, if thou wilt go down into the wilderness to my father, thou shalt have place with us.

And it came to pass that Zoram did take courage at the words which I spake. Now Zoram was the name of the servant; and he promised that he would go down into the wilderness unto our father. And he also made an oath unto us, that he would tarry with us from that time forth.

links.text: Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me.

provenance.alternative: An oath of attachment is a common enough biblical act; Ittai's at 2 Samuel 15:21 is closer in wording and was already cited for the doubled oath at 3:15.
provenance.significance: Ruth 1:16-17 is the KJV's model of an outsider binding herself by oath to a family in flight, and the Book of Mormon needs exactly that: Zoram is a servant of the enemy, incorporated by his own oath into a household leaving the land, and never again treated as anything but a brother (2 Nephi 1:30-32, where Lehi blesses him as a friend). The oath is what converts a hostage into a member.

links.note: 'He promised that he would go down into the wilderness unto our father. And he also made an oath unto us, that he would tarry with us from that time forth.' Nothing verbal survives, so this is proposed on function: the KJV's one scene of an outsider swearing permanent attachment to a departing family is Ruth's, and the Book of Mormon reproduces its effect — a person outside the covenant made a member of the household by an oath he volunteers.
links.whyNot: Zero shared wording, and the narrative situations differ at the point Ruth's oath is famous for: Ruth chooses a people and a God, Zoram chooses his life over death at the hands of the man who has just beheaded his master. The coercion is not in Ruth and cannot be argued away. Kept because the incorporation is permanent in both, and because the Book of Mormon later treats Zoram exactly as Ruth is treated.

pericopes.text: Now we were desirous that he should tarry with us for this cause: that the Jews might not know concerning our flight into the wilderness, lest they should pursue us and destroy us.
And it came to pass that when Zoram had made an oath unto us, our fears did cease concerning him.
And it came to pass that we took the plates of brass and the servant of Laban, and departed into the wilderness, and journied unto the tent of our father.

And it came to pass that after we had came down into the wilderness unto our father, behold he was filled with joy, and also my mother, Sariah, was exceeding glad, for she truly had mourned because of us;

for she had supposed that we had perished in the wilderness; and she also had complained against my father, telling him that he was a visionary man; saying, behold thou hast led us forth from the land of our inheritance, and my sons are no more, and we perish in the wilderness.

links.text: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him.

provenance.other: Four KJV verses have a mourner who refuses or will not be comforted: Genesis 37:35 (Jacob for Joseph), Psalm 77:2, Jeremiah 31:15 (Rachel for her children, 'because they were not') and Matthew 2:18, which quotes Jeremiah with the tense changed to 'because they are not'.
provenance.significance: The chapter itself supplies the reading. Sariah mourns sons she believes dead in a foreign errand, and at 5:14 the plates reveal that the family descends from Joseph — the son Jacob mourned as dead in exactly these words, and who was alive in Egypt the whole time. Genesis 37:35 is the parent's grief that the Joseph story exists to reverse, and 1 Nephi 5 reverses it in six verses: 'my sons are no more' at 5:2, 'my mother was comforted' at 5:7. Jacob refuses comfort and gets it only at Genesis 45:26; Sariah gets it when the sons walk in.

links.note: 'She had supposed that we had perished in the wilderness … my sons are no more.' The complaint is Jacob's at Genesis 37:35 and 42:36 ('Joseph is not, and Simeon is not'), and Rachel's at Jeremiah 31:15 — a parent grieving children who 'are not', where the reader knows they are. The Book of Mormon's phrase is 'are no more' rather than either KJV form, so no single verse is demonstrable on wording; what is demonstrable is that the chapter names Joseph nine verses later and makes the family his. Sariah's complaint is also the wilderness murmur of 2:11 in a different mouth — 'thou hast led us forth from the land of our inheritance' is what Laman said, and the narrative gives it to the mother without editorial comment.

pericopes.text: And after this manner of language had my mother complained against my father.

And it had came to pass that my father spake unto her saying: I know that I am a visionary man; for if I had not seen the things of God in a vision, I should not have known the goodness of God, but had tarried at Jerusalem and had perished with my brethren.

But behold, I have obtained a land of promise, in the which thing I do rejoice; yea, and I know that the Lord will deliver my sons out of the hands of Laban, and bring them down again unto us in the wilderness.

links.text: These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.

provenance.other: 'Land of promise' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:9; 11:13 is the sentence four verses later that explains how a promise can be possessed before it is received.
provenance.significance: Lehi says 'I have obtained a land of promise' while sitting in a tent in Arabia, having obtained nothing. Hebrews 11:13 is the verse that licenses the tense — the patriarchs 'died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off … and embraced them.' The Book of Mormon has now used Hebrews 11:8, 11:9, 11:13 and 11:29 in four chapters, in the source's own order, and the perfect tense in 5:5 is the clearest sign that the chapter is thinking in Hebrews 11's grammar of faith.

links.note: 'But behold, I have obtained a land of promise, in the which thing I do rejoice.' The phrase is Hebrews 11:9's, already catalogued at 2:20, and the completed aspect is Hebrews 11:13's doctrine: the promise is embraced and confessed as one's own while still seen afar off. Recorded here rather than folded into the 2:20 link because the tense is the point — Lehi is not repeating the promise, he is claiming it as already held, which is the specific claim Hebrews 11:13 makes about the patriarchs and which nothing in the Old Testament states.

pericopes.text: And after this manner of language did my father Lehi comfort my mother Sariah, concerning us, while we journied in the wilderness up to the land of Jerusalem, to obtain the record of the Jews.
And when we had returned to the tent of my father, behold their joy was full, and my mother was comforted;

and she spake, saying: Now I know of a surety that the Lord hath commanded my husband to flee into the wilderness; yea, and I also know of a surety that the Lord hath protected my sons and delivered them out of the hands of Laban, and gave them power whereby they could accomplish the thing which the Lord hath commanded them. And after this manner of language did she speak.

links.text: And when Peter was come to himself, he said, Now I know of a surety, that the LORD hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews.

provenance.other: 'Know of a surety' occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Genesis 15:13 has it as an imperative to Abram; Acts 12:11 is the only occurrence of the first-person declaration 'Now I know of a surety'.
provenance.significance: Sariah's speech reproduces not just the formula but the whole sentence Peter speaks on the far side of a deliverance: 'Now I know of a surety, that the LORD hath … delivered me out of the hand of Herod.' She says 'the Lord hath … delivered them out of the hands of Laban', with the tyrant's name substituted. And the deliverance she is talking about was announced by an angel at 3:29, as Peter's was performed by one. The two most confident statements of knowledge in the first five chapters — this and Lehi's at 5:4 — are both put in the mouth of the doubter, immediately after the doubt is answered.

links.note: 'Now I know of a surety that the Lord hath commanded my husband to flee into the wilderness; yea, and I also know of a surety that the Lord hath protected my sons and delivered them out of the hands of Laban.' The machine stream ranked this the highest-scoring candidate in 1 Nephi so far (rarity 5.04, a ten-word window), and for once the ranking is right: the phrase is unique to two verses, the first-person form to one, and the delivered-out-of-the-hand-of-X clause follows in both. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because a complete clause of one identifiable verse is reproduced with only the tyrant's name changed.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they did rejoice exceedingly, and did offer sacrifice and burnt offerings unto the Lord; and they gave thanks unto the God of Israel.
And after that they had given thanks unto the God of Israel, my father Lehi took the records which were engraven upon the plates of brass, and he did search them from the beginning.

links.text: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

provenance.alternative: 'Search' is an ordinary verb for reading a record and the Old Testament uses it of documents (Ezra 4:15, 6:1, 'search … in the book of the records').
provenance.significance: Two KJV verses make scripture the object of the verb 'search', and both are New Testament: John 5:39 as a command to opponents, Acts 17:11 as praise for hearers who check. Lehi's first act on obtaining the plates is the Berean act — he takes the record and searches it from the beginning — and 5:21 reports the verdict of the search ('we searched them and found that they were desirable'), which is Acts 17:11's structure exactly: search, then find.

links.note: 'My father Lehi took the records … and he did search them from the beginning.' The verb with scripture as its object is a New Testament idiom in the KJV, and Acts 17:11 supplies both the searching and the verdict that follows it at 5:21. Ezra's 'search … in the book of the records' (4:15) is the Old Testament alternative and is an archival search for a legal precedent, which is not what Lehi does.

pericopes.text: And he beheld that they did contain the five Books of Moses, which gave an account of the creation of the world, and also of Adam and Eve, which was our first parents;
and also a record of the Jews from the beginning, even down to the commencement of the reign of Zedekiah, King of Judah;

links.text: And it came to pass the same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, and in the fifth month, that Hananiah the son of Azur the prophet, which was of Gibeon, spake unto me in the house of the LORD, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying,

provenance.route: Jeremiah's dateline → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: An eight-word run, 'the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah', occurring in the KJV at Jeremiah 28:1 and 49:34 only.
provenance.significance: The same dateline that opened the book at 1:4 now closes the record the book was written to obtain. The brass plates run 'even down to the commencement of the reign of Zedekiah' — that is, they stop at the sentence with which 1 Nephi begins. The Book of Mormon presents itself as resuming a record precisely where the record it inherits leaves off, and it marks the seam with Jeremiah's formula at both ends.

links.note: The 1:4 link repeated, and the repetition is the finding. Nephi dates his father's call by Jeremiah's dateline and then reports that the brass plates end at the same date. Whether or not the writer noticed, the effect is a splice: the two records are joined at one verse of Jeremiah, and everything after it is the Book of Mormon's own. Note that 5:13 immediately names Jeremiah as the last prophet on the plates, which makes the join explicit.

pericopes.text: and also the prophecies of the Holy prophets, from the beginning, even down to the commencement of the reign of Zedekiah; and also many prophecies which have been spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah.

links.text: To fulfil the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths: for as long as she lay desolate she kept sabbath, to fulfil threescore and ten years.

provenance.route: 2 Chronicles 36:21-22 / Ezra 1:1 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'By the mouth of Jeremiah' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and all three are the same formula about the same prophecy: 2 Chronicles 36:21, 36:22 and Ezra 1:1.
provenance.significance: The three KJV verses that speak of prophecy 'by the mouth of Jeremiah' all concern one thing — the seventy years, the exile, and its end. They are the Old Testament's last words and the hinge on which the return turns. 1 Nephi 5:13 puts Jeremiah's prophecies at the end of the brass plates, which is where 2 Chronicles puts them at the end of its own book, and the family carrying them is going the other way: out, not back. See also 3:20, where 'by the mouth of all the holy prophets' comes from Acts 3:21 — the two 'mouth of' formulas in this book are both borrowed and both are about the whole prophetic deposit.

links.note: 'Many prophecies which have been spoken by the mouth of Jeremiah.' The formula belongs in the KJV to three verses, all of them the closing frame of Chronicles and the opening of Ezra. Its appearance here is chronologically pointed: on the book's own timeline the seventy years have not begun, so the plates can contain Jeremiah's prophecies but not the formula by which later scripture summarizes them.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that my father Lehi also found upon the plates of brass, a genealogy of his fathers; wherefore he knew that he was a descendant of Joseph; yea, even that Joseph which was the son of Jacob, which was sold into Egypt, and which was preserved by the hand of the Lord, that he might preserve his father Jacob and all his household from perishing with famine.

links.text: And the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him,

provenance.mt: Genesis 37:28 — 'and they … sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.'
provenance.route: Genesis 37-50 → Stephen's speech (Acts 7:9-14) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Genesis narrates the sale over several verses and never in this compression. Acts 7:9 gives the whole thing in one clause — 'sold Joseph into Egypt' — and Acts 7:14 supplies the sequel in another: Joseph 'called his father Jacob to him, and all his kindred'.
provenance.significance: Third confirmed borrowing from Stephen's speech in five chapters, after 2:22 and 3:29, and the pattern is now a finding rather than a coincidence. Acts 7 is a compressed retelling of Israel's whole history organized around one thesis — that the deliverer his brethren reject is the one God sends — and 1 Nephi is a narrative built on that thesis, told by a younger brother his elder brothers refuse. The Book of Mormon does not merely quote Stephen; it takes his argument, his summaries, and his order (Abraham, Joseph, Moses), and 5:14-15 runs Joseph and the Exodus in two verses exactly as Acts 7:9-36 does.

links.note: 'Even that Joseph which was the son of Jacob, which was sold into Egypt, and which was preserved by the hand of the Lord, that he might preserve his father Jacob and all his household from perishing with famine.' The summary is Stephen's, not Genesis's: 'sold Joseph into Egypt' is Acts 7:9's clause, and the sending for Jacob 'and all his kindred' is Acts 7:14's. The preservation formula is Joseph's own at Genesis 45:7 and 50:20 ('to save much people alive'). Note also the genealogical relative: the 1830 reads 'that Joseph which was the son of Jacob', which is the KJV's genealogical idiom at Luke 3:34 ('which was the son of Jacob'), and 1920 modernized every 'which' in the verse to 'who' — so the first edition wears its source and the current text does not.

pericopes.text: And they were also led out of captivity and out of the land of Egypt, by that same God who had preserved them.
And thus my father Lehi did discover the genealogy of his fathers. And Laban also was a descendant of Joseph, wherefore he and his fathers had kept the records.
And now when my father saw all these things, he was filled with the spirit, and began to prophesy concerning his seed;
that these plates of brass should go forth unto all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people which were of his seed.

links.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: The fourfold formula — nation, kindred, tongue, people — is Revelation's and no other book's. It occurs at Revelation 5:9, 7:9, 11:9, 13:7, 14:6 and 17:15, with the members reordered, and nowhere in the Old Testament.
provenance.significance: Lehi's prophecy over the brass plates is that they 'should go forth unto all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people', and the KJV sentence he is speaking is the one about an angel carrying the everlasting gospel to exactly that audience. The Book of Mormon's own account of its transmission is therefore stated, at its first mention, in the words of the verse from which the whole apocalyptic missionary programme comes — and chapters 13 and 14, where Nephi sees the book carried to the Gentiles, will use the formula again. This is a case where the borrowed phrase is also the borrowed self-understanding.

links.note: 'That these plates of brass should go forth unto all nations, kindreds, tongues, and people.' The fourfold list is Revelation's signature and appears nowhere else in the English Bible. Which occurrence is in view is settled by content: 14:6 is the only one where the audience is being reached by a message carried to it, which is what Lehi is prophesying. The link also anchors the Revelation network that 1 Nephi 11-14 will run at length.

pericopes.text: Wherefore he said that these plates of brass should never perish; neither should they be dimmed any more by time. And he prophesied many things concerning his seed.

links.text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.

provenance.alternative: 'Should never perish' and 'dimmed by time' are not KJV phrases; the imperishability of a written record could be asserted without any source.
