provenance.significance: Isaiah 40:8 is the KJV's statement that the word outlasts what carries it, and 1 Peter 1:24-25 quotes it to say that this abiding word is the gospel preached. Lehi applies the claim to a physical object — plates of brass that 'should never perish; neither should they be dimmed any more by time' — which is a material reading of a figure about permanence. Isaiah 40 is also the chapter Lehi quotes at 1 Nephi 10:8, so the family's prophet is demonstrably working in it.

links.note: Recorded as an echo because nothing is reproduced. The claim of an imperishable word belongs in the KJV to Isaiah 40:8 and its New Testament citation, and Lehi is stating it of the plates. What tips it above a bare resemblance is that Isaiah 40 is a chapter this family uses — 10:8 quotes Isaiah 40:3 — and that 'dimmed' has no biblical source at all, which suggests a writer working from the idea rather than from a phrase.
links.whyNot: Zero verbal contact, and the two claims differ in kind: Isaiah says God's word outlasts flesh and grass, Lehi says a set of metal plates will not corrode or fade. A reader could take the verse as an unsourced prophecy about an artifact and lose nothing.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that thus far I and my father had kept the commandments wherewith the Lord had commanded us.

And we had obtained the record which the Lord had commanded us, and searched them and found that they were desirable; yea, even of great worth unto us, insomuch that we could preserve the commandments of the Lord unto our children.

links.text: More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.

provenance.alternative: 'Desirable' and 'of great worth' are ordinary evaluative words, and a family might praise a hard-won record without reaching for the Psalter.
provenance.significance: The plot has already made the comparison literal. At 3:24 the brothers offer Laban all their gold and silver for the plates; at 3:26 they lose the gold and silver and get nothing; at 4:38 they leave with the plates and no property at all. Psalm 19:10 says of the law that it is 'more to be desired … than gold, yea, than much fine gold', and Psalm 119:72 that 'the law of thy mouth is better unto me than thousands of gold and silver'. 1 Nephi 5:21's verdict — 'they were desirable; yea, even of great worth unto us' — is the Psalter's valuation delivered after the transaction has been performed on stage. The book has dramatized a metaphor and then quoted it.

links.note: 'We had obtained the record which the Lord had commanded us, and searched them and found that they were desirable; yea, even of great worth unto us.' No phrase is reproduced, so this rests on the fit between the Psalter's standing comparison and the chapter's completed exchange. It is recorded at high confidence anyway, because the exchange is not incidental: two chapters were spent losing the gold in order to gain the law, which is Psalm 19:10 and Psalm 119:72 acted out.

pericopes.text: Wherefore it was wisdom in the Lord that we should carry them with us, as we journied in the wilderness towards the land of promise.

And now I, Nephi, do not give the genealogy of my fathers in this part of my record; neither at any time shall I give it after upon these plates which I am writing; for it is given in the record which has been kept by my father; wherefore I do not write it in this work.
For it sufficeth me to say, that we are a descendant of Joseph.

And it mattereth not to me that I am particular to give a full account of all the things of my father, for they cannot be written upon these plates, for I desire the room, that I may write of the things of God.

links.text: And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

provenance.alternative: The apology for an abridged record is a convention of ancient historiography generally, not a Johannine property; 2 Maccabees 2:24-31 makes the same excuse at length and is not in the KJV.
provenance.significance: John's two colophons are the KJV's only formal statements that a record has been cut short for reasons of space and selection — 'many other signs truly did Jesus … which are not written in this book', and the hyperbole about the world not containing the books. 1 Nephi's editorial apparatus makes the same move repeatedly (1:16, 6:3, 9:2, 14:28), and it is the move that constitutes the Book of Mormon as a selected record with a stated purpose rather than a chronicle. Verse 4 then gives the purpose, exactly as John 20:31 does: 'these are written, that ye might believe.'

links.note: 'They cannot be written upon these plates, for I desire the room, that I may write of the things of God.' The gesture — too much material, deliberate omission, and a stated criterion of selection — is John's colophon, and the two verses run in John's order: the omission at 6:3, then the purpose clause at 6:4 answering John 20:31. Nothing verbal is reproduced; the physical constraint ('I desire the room') is the Book of Mormon's own, and is the point at which its metal plates make the convention literal.

pericopes.text: For the fullness of mine intent is that I may persuade men to come unto the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and be saved.

links.text: Saying, I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Then Moses trembled, and durst not behold.

provenance.mt: Exodus 3:6 — 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (also 3:15, 4:5, identically).
provenance.route: Exodus 3:6 → the New Testament citation form (Matthew 22:32 / Mark 12:26 / Luke 20:37 / Acts 7:32) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The two English forms differ by one word. All three Exodus verses read 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'; all four New Testament verses read 'the God of Abraham, AND the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'. 1 Nephi 6:4 has the second 'and'.
provenance.alternative: The four New Testament verses are identical across the whole shared span, so nothing in the wording selects among them. Acts 7:32 is named as source because Stephen's speech is a demonstrated source for this book at 2:22, 3:29 and 5:14; the three Synoptic verses are kept as composite and a reader may prefer any of them.
provenance.significance: A second clean mediation test, decided the same way as 2:22 and by the same kind of evidence — a single word that differs between the Old Testament KJV and its New Testament quotation. Fourteen words are reproduced in sequence, which is the longest verbatim run in 1 Nephi 1-6, and they are reproduced in the New Testament's form. The Book of Mormon states the covenant name of God in the wording it has in the mouth of Jesus and of Stephen, not in the wording it has at the burning bush.

links.note: 'That I may persuade men to come unto the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and be saved.' Fourteen words verbatim, and the second conjunction is the whole argument: Exodus never has it and the New Testament always does. Still below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations — worth saying, because on run length alone this is the closest 1 Nephi 1-6 comes to it. See 6:5 for the Pauline frame the sentence sits in; 'persuade men' in 6:4 and 'pleasing' in 6:5 are both Galatians 1:10's.

pericopes.text: Wherefore the things which are pleasing unto the world, I do not write, but the things which are pleasing unto God and unto them which are not of the world.

links.text: For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.

provenance.other: 'Persuade men' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 1:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:11. 'Please men' / 'pleased men' occurs in exactly one, Galatians 1:10. That one verse therefore contains both of the terms 1 Nephi 6:4-5 uses, and is the only verse in the English Bible that does.
provenance.significance: Two consecutive Book of Mormon verses take their two governing terms from one Pauline sentence, and take them in Paul's order. Galatians 1:10 asks whether the writer persuades men or God and whether he seeks to please men; 1 Nephi 6:4 says his intent is to persuade men, and 6:5 says he writes not what pleases the world but what pleases God. Recover Galatians 1:10's context and the point sharpens: Paul is defending the independent authority of his gospel — 'I neither received it of man, neither was I taught it, but by the revelation of Jesus Christ' (1:12) — which is the claim Nephi's colophon has been making since 1:3.

links.note: 'The things which are pleasing unto the world, I do not write, but the things which are pleasing unto God and unto them which are not of the world.' Set against Galatians 1:10, the two rare terms of 6:4-5 belong to a single verse, and the antithesis is Paul's: men or God, pleasing men or serving Christ. The Book of Mormon adds the third party — 'them which are not of the world' — which is Johannine rather than Pauline (John 15:19, 17:14), and which is how the colophon includes its own readers. The 1830 'them which' is the KJV relative; 1920 reads 'those who'.

pericopes.text: Wherefore I shall give commandment unto my seed, that they shall not occupy these plates with things which are not of worth unto the children of men.

And now I would that ye might know, that after my father Lehi had made an end of prophesying concerning his seed, it came to pass that the Lord spake unto him again, saying, that it was not mete for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone; but that his sons should take daughters to wife, that they might raise up seed unto the Lord in the land of promise.

links.text: And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.

provenance.other: 'Help meet' occurs in two KJV verses, Genesis 2:18 and 2:20, and 'should be alone' in one. The 1830 spells the Book of Mormon's word 'mete', which 1920 corrected to 'meet' — the KJV's own spelling and the KJV's own word.
provenance.significance: The Lord's reason for sending the sons back to Jerusalem is stated in the Lord's own words for making Eve: it is not good, not meet, for the man to be alone. The Book of Mormon has taken the two load-bearing words of Genesis 2:18 — the negation and 'meet' — and rebuilt the sentence around a family rather than a person. The purpose clause then reaches for the levirate formula ('raise up seed', Genesis 38:8 and its three New Testament quotations) and redirects it from a dead brother to the Lord.

links.note: 'It was not mete for him, Lehi, that he should take his family into the wilderness alone; but that his sons should take daughters to wife, that they might raise up seed unto the Lord in the land of promise.' The KJV's 'It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him' supplies the negation, the aloneness and the adjective, and the 1830's 'mete' is the KJV's spelling of it. Note that 'raise up seed' is the levirate phrase of Genesis 38:8, quoted in the New Testament at Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:19 and Luke 20:28 — the Sadducees' resurrection question, whose next verses gave 1 Nephi 6:4 its formula for the God of Abraham.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord commanded him that I, Nephi, and my brethren, should again return unto the land of Jerusalem, and bring down Ishmael and his family into the wilderness.
And it came to pass that I, Nephi, did again, with my brethren, go forth into the wilderness to go up to Jerusalem.
And it came to pass that we went up unto the house of Ishmael, and we did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael, insomuch that we did, speak unto him the words of the Lord.

links.text: But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.

provenance.alternative: 'Favour in the sight of' occurs in seven KJV verses, including Esther's twice, and is the standard idiom for winning someone over.
provenance.significance: Two of the seven occurrences carry weight here. Genesis 39:21 is Joseph — the ancestor this family has just discovered itself to have (5:14) — winning favour in a foreign house while a prisoner. Exodus 3:21 and 12:36 are the LORD giving Israel favour in the sight of the Egyptians so that they may leave the country carrying what they need. 1 Nephi 7:4 is a party from the wilderness winning over a Jerusalem household in order to take it out of the city; both senses fit, and the Book of Mormon is doing at 7:4 what the Exodus verses do and doing it in Joseph's phrase.

links.note: 'We did gain favor in the sight of Ishmael.' The idiom is common enough that the link rests on context rather than rarity, and the context is thick: the chapter before has just established the family's descent from Joseph, and Joseph is the KJV's figure for gaining favour in a household not one's own. Verse 5 then adds the softened heart, which is the Book of Mormon's own answer to Exodus's hardened one.

pericopes.text: Andto itthe cametent toof passour thatfather .the Lord did soften the heart of Ishmael, and also his household, insomuch that they took their journey with us down into the wilderness

And it came to pass that as we journied in the wilderness, behold, Laman and Lemuel, and two of the daughters of Ishmael, and the two sons of Ishmael, and their families, did rebel against us; yea, against I, Nephi, and Sam, and their father, Ishmael, and his wife, and his three other daughters.
And it came to pass in the which rebellion, they were desirous to return unto the land of Jerusalem.

links.text: Wherefore she went forth out of the place where she was, and her two daughters in law with her; and they went on the way to return unto the land of Judah.

provenance.other: 'Return unto the land of' occurs in four KJV verses (Genesis 31:3, 31:13, Joshua 1:15, Ruth 1:7). Only Ruth 1:7 has daughters travelling with a family and facing the choice whether to go back.
provenance.significance: Ruth 1 is the KJV's one narrative about daughters attached by marriage to a migrating household, some of whom turn back and some of whom cleave. 1 Nephi 7:6-7 divides Ishmael's daughters the same way — two rebel and are 'desirous to return unto the land of Jerusalem', three stay — and at 7:19 it is one of the daughters who intervenes to save Nephi's life. The book has already used Ruth's oath of attachment for Zoram at 4:35; it is using her narrative here.

links.note: 'They were desirous to return unto the land of Jerusalem.' The four-word phrase is one of four KJV occurrences, and the situation selects Ruth's: a household leaving its land, with in-law daughters who must choose. Orpah's return is the exact shape of what two of Ishmael's daughters attempt, and the chapter resolves as Ruth 1 does, by some of them cleaving.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, therefore I spake unto them, saying; yea, even unto Laman and unto Lemuel, behold, thou art mine elder brethren; and how is it that ye are so hard in your hearts, and so blind in your minds, that ye have need that I, your younger brother, should speak unto you, yea, and set an example for you?

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: 'Hardness of their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 1 Nephi 7:8 reproduces seven consecutive words of it, including the preposition — 'being grieved for the hardness of their hearts' — where 1 Nephi 2:18 had 'because of'.
provenance.significance: The second occurrence is closer than the first, which settles the case. At 2:18 the clause was 'being grieved because of the hardness of their hearts', which a sceptic could call convergent phrasing; here it is Mark's exact seven words in Mark's exact order, and the two Book of Mormon verses describe the same two brothers. And in both, Mark's context supplies the reading: it is Jesus, in the synagogue, grieved at men who are watching to see whether he will do something they can accuse him of. Verse 16 has them bind Nephi with cords.

links.note: 'And now I, Nephi, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts.' Verbatim from the only KJV verse in which the phrase exists, and one of the highest-ranked machine candidates in the book (rarity 4.50, an eight-word window). This is the one link in 1 Nephi 1-7 recorded at 'certain': the clause is unique in the English Bible, it is reproduced without alteration, and it has already appeared once in the same book about the same people. The rest of the verse continues the borrowing loosely — 'so blind in your minds' is 2 Corinthians 4:4's 'blinded the minds', and the anaphora of 7:9-12 ('How is it that ye …', four times) is the shape of Jesus's chain of reproaches at Mark 8:17-21.

pericopes.text: How is it that ye have not hearkened unto the word of the Lord?
How is it that ye have forgotten that ye have seen an angel of the Lord?

links.text: And when Gideon perceived that he was an angel of the LORD, Gideon said, Alas, O LORD God! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face.

provenance.other: 'Have seen an angel of the LORD' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Gideon's reaction to having seen the angel is terror at the consequences of the sight; Laman and Lemuel's, on Nephi's account, is to forget it. The rebuke works by the contrast the source supplies — in the KJV the sight of an angel is the sort of thing that makes a man cry 'Alas, O LORD God!', and these two have mislaid it in seven verses.

links.note: 'How is it that ye have forgotten that ye have seen an angel of the Lord?' The seven-word clause exists once in the KJV. The angel in question is the one of 3:29, and the rebuke turns on the KJV's own valuation of such an experience rather than on Gideon's story in particular.

pericopes.text: Yea, and how is it that ye have forgotten how great things the Lord hath done for us, in delivering us out of the hands of Laban, and also that we should obtain the record?

links.text: Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.

provenance.other: 'How great things' occurs in five KJV verses (1 Samuel 12:24, Mark 5:19, 5:20, Luke 8:39, Acts 9:16). Only Mark 5:19 reads 'how great things the LORD hath done for'. Luke 8:39, the parallel, reads 'how great things GOD hath done unto thee'.
provenance.significance: This is a first-edition case of the kind §8 exists for, and the cleanest one so far. The 1830 reads 'how great things the Lord hath done for us', which is Mark 5:19 word for word. The 1920 edition changed 'how' to 'what' — 'what great things the Lord hath done for us' — which is not in the KJV at all. So the first edition preserves an eight-word quotation of Mark and every subsequent edition has partly erased it. The catalogue can only see this because it runs on the 1830 text.

links.note: 'How is it that ye have forgotten how great things the Lord hath done for us, in delivering us out of the hands of Laban.' Eight words of Mark 5:19, in order, in the 1830. Mark's sentence is the commission given to the healed Gerasene — go and tell how great things the Lord hath done for thee — and Nephi is using it as a reproach for not having told, or not having remembered. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule. The 1830/1920 divergence is recorded under significance and is the reason this link would be invisible in the current text.

pericopes.text: Yea, and how is it that ye have forgotten that the Lord is able to do all things, according to his will, for the children of men, if it so be that they exercise faith in him; wherefore, let us be faithful in him.

links.text: Jesus said unto him, If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.

provenance.alternative: Divine omnipotence conditioned on faith is a commonplace; Daniel 3:17 ('our God … is able to deliver us'), already used at 1 Nephi 4:3, would account for the ability clause on its own.
provenance.significance: What Mark 9:23 adds to the ability formula is the condition, and the condition is what 7:12 has: 'the Lord is able to do all things … if it so be that they exercise faith in him.' In Mark the sentence is addressed to a father whose son the disciples could not heal, and the answer is 'Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief' — the exact posture Nephi is trying to argue his brothers into.

links.note: 'The Lord is able to do all things, according to his will, for the children of men, if it so be that they exercise faith in him.' Ability plus a faith condition; the KJV's version is Mark 9:23, with Matthew 19:26 and Mark 10:27 supplying the unconditioned form. Recorded as an echo because no phrase survives, and at moderate because the conditional is the distinctive element and it is Mark's.

pericopes.text: And if it so be that we are faithful in him, we shall obtain the land of promise; and ye shall know at some future period, that the word of the Lord shall be fulfilled, concerning the destruction of Jerusalem; for all things which the Lord hath spoken concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, must be fulfilled.

For, behold, the spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them; for behold, they have rejected the prophets, and Jeremiah have they cast into prison. And they have sought to take away the life of my father, insomuch that they have driven him out of the land.

links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.other: The collocation of the divine spirit with the verb 'strive' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence that begins the flood — the withdrawal of divine forbearance, with a term of years attached, immediately before the destruction of everyone outside one family's boat. 1 Nephi 7:14 uses it to announce the destruction of Jerusalem, in a book whose one family is about to leave in a boat of its own (18:8). The typology is not stated and does not have to be; the borrowed clause carries the flood with it.

links.note: 'For, behold, the spirit of the Lord ceaseth soon to strive with them.' The KJV joins God's spirit to striving once, at Genesis 6:3, and the Book of Mormon reproduces the collocation with the temporal qualifier intact — 'not always' becoming 'ceaseth soon'. The rest of the verse is contemporary Jerusalem rather than allusion: the prophets rejected, Jeremiah in prison (Jeremiah 32:2, 37:15, 38:6), and Lehi driven out.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 7.14 (Jeremiah 32:1-2, for the imprisonment of Jeremiah)

pericopes.text: Now, behold, I say unto you, that if ye will return unto Jerusalem, ye shall also perish with them. And now, if ye have choice, go up to the land, and remember the words which I speak unto you, that if ye go, ye will also perish; for thus the spirit of the Lord constraineth me that I should speak.

links.text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

provenance.alternative: Offering an audience a free choice with a stated consequence is the standard shape of a covenant address and needs no single source.
provenance.significance: Joshua 24:15 is the KJV's set-piece of the freely offered alternative: choose, and here is where I stand. 1 Nephi 7:15 makes the same offer with the consequence attached — 'if ye have choice, go up to the land … if ye go, ye will also perish' — and then, like Joshua, declines to soften it. The clause that follows is the giveaway that this is a formal speech and not a quarrel: 'thus the spirit of the Lord constraineth me that I should speak.'

links.note: Proposed on form. Nothing verbal is shared; what is shared is the covenant-address structure of a genuine choice with an announced outcome, which the KJV states most memorably at Joshua 24:15. Recorded at moderate because 1 Nephi 7:15 does the same work in the same order and because the chapter's argument has otherwise been Deuteronomic since verse 9.
links.whyNot: No shared wording at all, and the two speeches differ at the centre: Joshua's choice is between gods, Nephi's is between two destinations. A reader could decline this without losing anything the chapter needs.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when I, Nephi, had spoken these words unto my brethren, they were angry with me. And it came to pass that they did lay their hands upon me; for, behold, they were exceeding wroth; and they did bind me with cords, for they sought to take away my life, that they might leave me in the wilderness, to be devoured by wild beasts.

links.text: Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into some pit, and we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

provenance.significance: The Joseph cycle, running since the dream formula at 3:2 and made explicit by the genealogy at 5:14, arrives at its central scene. Brothers seize the younger, leave him in a wilderness place, and intend a wild beast to account for the body — 'we will say, Some evil beast hath devoured him.' 1 Nephi 7:16 states the plan as fact rather than as cover story: they bound him 'that they might leave me in the wilderness, to be devoured by wild beasts'. Genesis 37 also supplies the intercession at 7:19 (Reuben) and the forgiveness at 7:20-21 (Genesis 50), so the chapter runs the whole arc from pit to reconciliation in six verses.

links.note: 'They did bind me with cords, for they sought to take away my life, that they might leave me in the wilderness, to be devoured by wild beasts.' No phrase is reproduced, but the plan is Genesis 37:20's in every element, including the beast — which in Genesis is a lie the brothers rehearse and here is the method itself. The elder-brothers-against-the-dreamer frame has been in place since 2:11, and this is the scene it was pointing at.

pericopes.text: But it came to pass that I prayed unto the Lord, saying: O Lord, according to my faith which is in thee, wilt thou deliver me from the hands of my brethren; yea, even give me strength that I may burst these bands with which I am bound.

links.text: And Samson called unto the LORD, and said, O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.

provenance.significance: A bound man prays for strength and his bonds come off. That is Samson's story twice over — cords at Judges 15:13-14, and the prayer for strength at 16:28 — and 1 Nephi 7:17-18 runs both halves in two verses. See 7:18 for what makes the borrowing demonstrable rather than merely apt.

links.note: 'Wilt thou deliver me from the hands of my brethren; yea, even give me strength that I may burst these bands with which I am bound.' The prayer is Samson's petition of Judges 16:28 with the vengeance removed, and the situation is Judges 15:13, where Samson is bound with cords by his own countrymen and handed over. Recorded at high on the strength of the verbal case at the next verse.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that when I had said these words, behold, the bands were loosed from off my hands and feet, and I stood before my brethren, and I spake unto them again.

links.text: And when he came unto Lehi, the Philistines shouted against him: and the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the cords that were upon his arms became as flax that was burnt with fire, and his bands loosed from off his hands.

provenance.other: 'Bands loosed from off his hands' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. So does the name Lehi — or rather, the name Lehi occurs in exactly three, Judges 15:9, 15:14 and 15:19, and they are the only three verses in the entire King James Bible where the word appears.
provenance.significance: This is the finding of the chapter and possibly of the book. 1 Nephi 7:18 reproduces the distinctive clause of Judges 15:14 — a bound man's bands loosed from off his hands after the Spirit comes on him — and Judges 15:14 opens with the words 'And when he came unto Lehi.' The one KJV verse the Book of Mormon demonstrably borrows here is one of the only three KJV verses containing the name of the Book of Mormon's founding patriarch. Judges 15 also supplies, at 15:19, God cleaving a hollow place so that water comes out for a man about to perish of thirst, 'which is in Lehi unto this day' — and 1 Nephi 2:6-9 puts Lehi at a river in a valley and 1 Nephi 17:29 has Moses smite the rock for water. The catalogue records the coincidence and does not explain it; explaining it is a different kind of book. But no reader of this project should have to find it for themselves.

links.note: 'The bands were loosed from off my hands and feet.' Six words reproducing the sole KJV occurrence, with 'his' changed to 'my' and 'and feet' added. The whole scene is Judges 15:13-14: bound with cords by his own people, and freed when the Spirit comes. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations. The observation about the name — Lehi is a KJV word only in Judges 15, and this is Judges 15 — belongs to the provenance note above and is stated there as an observation, not an argument.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were angry with me again, and sought to lay hands upon me; but, behold, one of the daughters of Ishmael, yea, and also her mother, and one of the sons of Ishmael did plead with my brethren, insomuch that they did soften their hearts; and they did cease striving to take away my life.

links.text: And Reuben heard it, and he delivered him out of their hands; and said, Let us not kill him.

provenance.significance: Genesis 37 does not let the murder happen: Reuben intervenes, then Judah, and the brother is sold rather than killed. 1 Nephi 7:19 supplies the same structural mercy from a different quarter — one of Ishmael's daughters, her mother, and one of his sons — which redistributes the Genesis role to the in-laws and to a woman. The intercession is what makes the reconciliation of 7:20-21 possible, exactly as it is in Genesis.

links.note: 'One of the daughters of Ishmael, yea, and also her mother, and one of the sons of Ishmael did plead with my brethren, insomuch that they did soften their hearts.' The Joseph plot requires an intercessor at precisely this point and the Book of Mormon provides three. Nothing verbal is shared; the case is the position of the scene in a sequence the chapter has already committed to at 7:16.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they were sorrowful, because of their wickedness, insomuch that they did bow down before me, and did plead with me, that I would forgive them of the thing that they had done against me.

links.text: So shall ye say unto Joseph, Forgive, I pray thee now, the trespass of thy brethren, and their sin; for they did unto thee evil: and now, we pray thee, forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father. And Joseph wept when they spake unto him.

provenance.significance: The Joseph arc closes in the same chapter it opened. Brothers who intended his death bow before him and beg forgiveness for 'the thing that they had done against me', which is Genesis 50:17's 'the trespass of thy brethren … for they did unto thee evil'; the prostration is Genesis 50:18 and 42:6, 'his brethren also went and fell down before his face'; and the forgiveness is Genesis 50:21, where Joseph comforts them and speaks kindly. 1 Nephi 7 has run pit, intercession, reconciliation — Genesis 37 and 50 — inside five verses, which is the whole Joseph novella compressed into an episode of a journey.

links.note: 'They did bow down before me, and did plead with me, that I would forgive them of the thing that they had done against me.' The scene is Genesis 50:17-18 with the roles held constant. What the Book of Mormon does not take is Joseph's theology of it — 'ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good' (50:20) — which would have justified the brothers' hostility as providential. Nephi's answer at 7:21 is simply forgiveness, and it comes in Luke's words rather than Genesis's.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I did frankly forgive them all that they had done, and I did exhort them that they would pray unto the Lord their God, for forgiveness. And it came to pass that they did so. And after that they had done praying unto the Lord, we did again travel on our journey toward the tent of our father.

links.text: And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?

provenance.other: 'Frankly' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it occurs there as 'frankly forgave'. The adverb is used nowhere else in the English Bible.
provenance.significance: A word that exists once in the King James Bible turns up in the Book of Mormon attached to the same verb. Luke 7:42 is the parable of the two debtors, told to a Pharisee to explain why a forgiven woman loves much — 'to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.' Nephi forgives brothers who had just bound him to die, and the adverb he is given for it is the one Jesus uses for a creditor who cancels a debt neither man could pay. The Genesis 50 scene supplies the situation and Luke 7:42 supplies the single most distinctive word in the sentence.

links.note: 'I did frankly forgive them all that they had done.' 'Frankly' is a KJV hapax and it is bound to this verb in its one occurrence, which makes the borrowing about as demonstrable as a single word can be. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because only the adverb-and-verb survive; the surrounding clause is Genesis 50's (see 7:20).

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that we did come down unto the tent of our father. And after that I and my brethren, and all the house of Ishmael, had come down unto the tent of my father, they did give thanks unto the Lord their God; and they did offer sacrifice and burnt offerings unto him.
And it came to pass that we had gathered together all manner of seeds of every kind; both of grain of every kind, and also of the seeds of fruits of every kind.
And it came to pass that while my father tarried in the wilderness, he spake unto us, saying: Behold, I have dreamed a dream; or, in other words, I have seen a vision.

And behold, because of the thing which I have seen, I have reason to rejoice in the Lord, because of Nephi, and also of Sam; for I have reason to suppose that they, and also many of their seed, will be saved.—
But, behold, Laman and Lemuel, I fear exceedingly, because of you; for, behold, me thought I saw a dark and dreary wilderness.
And it came to pass that I saw a man, and he was dressed in a white robe; and he came and stood before me.

links.text: After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;

provenance.other: 'White robe' or 'white robes' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them Revelation (6:11, 7:9, 7:13). The guide who bids the seer follow is Ezekiel's (40:3-4, 'he brought me thither, and, behold, there was a man') and Revelation's own (17:1, 21:9).
provenance.significance: Lehi's dream opens with the two conventions the visionary literature runs on, and takes both from the KJV's apocalypses. The white robe belongs to Revelation and nowhere else in the English Bible; the man who appears, speaks, and bids the seer follow is the guide of Ezekiel 40 and Revelation 17. Verse 21's 'numberless concourses of people' is then Revelation 7:9's other half — 'a great multitude, which no man could number' — from the same verse as the robe.

links.note: 'I saw a man, and he was dressed in a white robe; and he came and stood before me … and bade me follow him.' The garment is Revelation's, the office is Ezekiel's. Held at moderate because neither element is reproduced verbatim and both are conventions rather than quotations; what raises it above bare convention is that the same verse, Revelation 7:9, also supplies the innumerable multitude at 8:21 and the fourfold formula already catalogued at 5:18.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he spake unto me, and bade me follow him.
And it came to pass that as I followed him, and after I had followed him, I beheld myself that I was in a dark and dreary waste.
And after that I had travelled for the space of many hours in darkness, I began to pray unto the Lord, that he would have mercy on me, according to the multitude of his tender mercies.

links.text: Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.

provenance.other: 'The multitude of thy tender mercies' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 51:1 and Psalm 69:16, and both are petitions for mercy from inside distress.
provenance.significance: The book's signature phrase returns to its source. 1 Nephi 1:20 gave 'the tender mercies of the Lord are over all them whom he hath chosen', which is Psalm 145:9's; here the phrase arrives with its Psalter frame intact — the whole clause, the preposition, and the petitionary setting of Psalm 51. Lehi lost in the dark prays the Miserere, which is the KJV's prayer of a man who knows he is at fault, and the dream then shows him two of his sons refusing the fruit.

links.note: 'I began to pray unto the Lord, that he would have mercy on me, according to the multitude of his tender mercies.' Eight words of Psalm 51:1 in sequence, with only the pronoun changed, and the petition ('have mercy … according to') reproduced from the same verse's opening. The Book of Mormon's most characteristic phrase, 'tender mercies', is the KJV's, and this is the verse that shows which part of the Psalter it comes from.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after I had prayed unto the Lord, I beheld a large and spacious field.
And it came to pass that I beheld a tree, whose fruit was desirable, to make one happy.

links.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.

provenance.other: 'To be desired to make one' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the word that completes it there is 'wise'. 1 Nephi 8:10 completes it with 'happy'.
provenance.significance: One word is changed and the whole theology of the dream turns on it. Genesis 3:6 describes the tree that must not be eaten — desirable to make one wise — and eating it is the fall. 1 Nephi 8:10 describes a tree that must be eaten — desirable to make one happy — and Lehi's whole distress is that two of his sons will not eat. The Book of Mormon takes the sentence of the forbidden tree and attaches it to the tree of life, and the sequel confirms the intent: 8:11-12 keeps Genesis 3:6's next movement, 'she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband' — Lehi partakes and then immediately desires that his family should partake also.

links.note: 'I beheld a tree, whose fruit was desirable, to make one happy.' Seven words of Genesis 3:6 with 'wise' replaced by 'happy', from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. The chapter then runs the rest of Genesis 3:6's clause — partaking, and giving to the family (8:11-12) — and pairs the tree with a river as Genesis 2:9-10 does, so that both Eden trees and the Eden river are in play at once. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because a phrase unique to a single KJV verse is reproduced with one substitution.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I did go forth, and partake of the fruit thereof; and I beheld that it was most sweet, above all that I ever had before tasted. Yea, and I beheld that the fruit thereof was white, to exceed all the whiteness that I had ever seen.

links.text: And his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow; so as no fuller on earth can white them.

provenance.alternative: Superlative whiteness is a standing figure of the visionary literature (Daniel 7:9, 'whose garment was white as snow'); the Book of Mormon's construction is its own.
provenance.significance: Mark 9:3's distinctive move is not the whiteness but the exhaustion of comparison — 'so as no fuller on earth can white them', a whiteness beyond what the world can produce. 1 Nephi 8:11 makes the same move by a different route: 'white, to exceed all the whiteness that I had ever seen.' The vision then repeats it at 11:8, where the tree's whiteness 'did exceed the whiteness of the driven snow', which is closer to Mark and Daniel both.

links.note: Recorded on the figure rather than the wording: a whiteness stated by exceeding every available comparison, which the KJV does at Mark 9:3 and Daniel 7:9. The same verse also has 'it filled my soul with exceeding great joy' at 8:12, and 'exceeding great joy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Matthew 2:10, the wise men at the star — which is noted here rather than catalogued separately because the phrase is doing ordinary intensifying work.

pericopes.text: And as I partook of the fruit thereof, it filled my soul with exceeding great joy; wherefore, I began to be desirous that my family should partake of it also; for I knew that it was desirous above all other fruit.
And as I cast my eyes round about, that perhaps I might discover my family also, I beheld a river of water; and it ran along, and it was near the tree of which I was partaking the fruit.

links.text: And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.

provenance.other: 'Tree of life' occurs in ten KJV verses — Genesis 2:9, 3:22, 3:24, four in Proverbs, and Revelation 2:7, 22:2, 22:14. Only two passages put the tree and a river in the same scene: Genesis 2:9-10 and Revelation 22:1-2.
provenance.significance: The dream's topography is the KJV's paradise topography, and it is the version at the end of the Bible rather than the one at the beginning. Revelation 22:1-2 has an angel who shews the seer a river proceeding from the throne, with the tree of life beside it — which is the guide of 8:5, the river of 8:13, and the tree of 8:10 in one place. Genesis supplies the tree's description (3:6, see 8:10) and Revelation supplies the arrangement. When Nephi is shown the same vision at 11:25 he calls the water 'the fountain of living waters', which is John 4:14 and Jeremiah 2:13, and at 15:26-29 he reinterprets the river as hell — so the family's readings of the same image diverge across the book, which is itself worth cataloguing.

links.note: 'I beheld a river of water; and it ran along, and it was near the tree of which I was partaking the fruit.' A tree beside a river, shown by an interpreting figure: that is Revelation 22:1-2 and, at one remove, Eden. The Psalter's version — 'like a tree planted by the rivers of water' (Psalm 1:3) — is kept in composite because Psalm 1 also supplies the scornful of 8:27 and the perishing way of 8:28, and may be governing more of the dream than this verse alone.

pericopes.text: And I looked to behold from whence it came; and I saw the head thereof, a little way off; and at the head thereof, I beheld your mother Sariah, and Sam, and Nephi; and they stood as if they knew not whither they should go.
And it came to pass that I beckoned unto them; and I also did say unto them, with a loud voice, that they should come unto me, and partake of the fruit, which was desirable above all other fruit.
And it came to pass that they did come unto me, and partake of the fruit also.
And it came to pass that I was desirous that Laman and Lemuel should come and partake of the fruit also; wherefore, I cast mine eyes towards the head of the river, that perhaps I might see them.
And it came to pass that I saw them, but they would not come unto me.
And I beheld a rod of iron; and it extended along the bank of the river, and led to the tree by which I stood.

links.text: And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.

provenance.route: Psalm 2:9 → Revelation → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: 'Rod of iron' occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Psalm 2:9 ('Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel') and its three quotations in Revelation (2:27, 12:5, 19:15), all of which read 'rule them with a rod of iron'.
provenance.significance: The transformation is the finding. In every one of its four KJV occurrences the rod of iron is a weapon — an instrument of shattering or of coercive rule over the nations, held by the Messiah or by those who overcome. In Lehi's dream it is a handrail. People take hold of the end of it and cling to it through the dark, and at 11:25 and 15:23 Nephi identifies it as the word of God. The Book of Mormon has taken the KJV's most violent sceptre and turned it into something you hold onto to keep from getting lost, which is not a reading any of the four source verses supports and is the image the whole dream is remembered for.

links.note: 'I beheld a rod of iron; and it extended along the bank of the river, and led to the tree by which I stood.' The phrase belongs to four KJV verses, one Psalm and its three apocalyptic citations, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it exactly while reversing its function from breaking to guiding. Note that the rod runs beside the river and the path runs beside the rod — the dream lays its three borrowed elements in parallel lines.

pericopes.text: And I also beheld a straight and narrow path, which came along by the rod of iron, even to the tree by which I stood; and it also led by the head of the fountain, unto a large and spacious field, as if it had been a world;

links.text: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

provenance.other: 'Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The 1830 spells the Book of Mormon's adjective 'straight' — the homophone — and the confusion is itself evidence: 'strait' means narrow, and a text that writes 'straight and narrow' has heard the phrase rather than parsed it.
provenance.significance: Matthew 7:13-14 supplies the path and Matthew 7:26-27 supplies the building, so two of the dream's three structures come from the last twenty verses of the Sermon on the Mount, in the Sermon's own order. Matthew's way 'leadeth unto life'; Lehi's path leads to the tree of life. Matthew's is found by few; Lehi's is entered by many who then lose it in the mist. The dream is an expansion of a single Matthean paragraph into a landscape.

links.note: 'I also beheld a straight and narrow path, which came along by the rod of iron, even to the tree by which I stood.' The phrase is Matthew 7:14's, unique in the KJV, and 'which came along … even to the tree' answers Matthew's 'which leadeth unto life'. The 1830 spelling 'straight' is the tell — it is the spelling of a phrase received by ear, and every later edition keeps it, so this is one of the rare places where the first edition and the current text agree in departing from the King James word.

pericopes.text: and I saw numberless concourses of people; many of whom were pressing forward, that they might obtain the path which led unto the tree by which I stood.
And it came to pass that they did come forth, and commence in the path which led to the tree.

And it came to pass that there arose a mist of darkness, yea, even an exceeding great mist of darkness, insomuch that they which had commenced in the path, did lose their way, that they wandered off, and were lost.

links.text: These are wells without water, clouds that are carried with a tempest; to whom the mist of darkness is reserved for ever.

provenance.other: 'Mist of darkness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jude 13's parallel reads 'blackness of darkness'.
provenance.significance: Recovering 2 Peter 2:17's context turns the image inside out. There the mist of darkness is not a hazard on a path — it is a punishment 'reserved for ever' for false teachers who 'allure through the lusts of the flesh … those that were clean escaped from them that live in error' (2:18). The people 2 Peter is describing are exactly the people in the great and spacious building at 8:26-27, and the fate assigned to them is the weather Lehi's travellers get lost in. Nephi's own interpretation at 12:17 — 'the mists of darkness are the temptations of the devil' — is a reading of the borrowed phrase, not of the source verse.

links.note: 'There arose a mist of darkness, yea, even an exceeding great mist of darkness.' The phrase exists in one verse of the English Bible and the Book of Mormon reproduces it and then intensifies it. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation because the phrase is a KJV singleton reproduced without alteration.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I beheld others pressing forward; and they came forth, and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press forward through the mist of darkness, clinging to the rod of iron, even until they did come forth and partake of the fruit of the tree.
And after that they had partaken of the fruit of the tree, they did cast their eyes about as if they were ashamed.
And I also cast my eyes round about, and beheld, on the other side of the river of water, a great and spacious building; and it stood as it were in the air, high above the earth;

links.text: And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:

provenance.other: Matthew 7:27 ends 'and it fell: and great was the fall of it.' 1 Nephi 11:36 ends the building's story: 'and it fell, and the fall thereof was exceeding great.'
provenance.significance: The building and the path come from the same page. Matthew 7:13-14 gave the strait and narrow way at 8:20; Matthew 7:24-27 gives the house with no foundation here — and 1 Nephi 11:36 supplies the fall in Matthew's own words, 'great was the fall of it'. Lehi's building 'stood as it were in the air, high above the earth', which is the Book of Mormon's image for a house built on nothing: not sand, but no ground at all. The Sermon on the Mount's closing parable has been turned into a place with people in it.

links.note: 'A great and spacious building; and it stood as it were in the air, high above the earth.' Nothing is reproduced at this verse; the case is made three chapters later, when the same building falls in Matthew 7:27's wording (1 Nephi 11:36). Recorded here because this is where the structure enters the dream and because its neighbour on the same page of Matthew has already been used at 8:20.

pericopes.text: and it was filled with people, both old and young, both male and female; and their manner of dress was exceeding fine; and they were in the attitude of mocking and pointing their fingers towards those which had come at, and were partaking of the fruit.

links.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.

provenance.alternative: Scoffers are everywhere in the KJV (Proverbs' scorner, 2 Peter 3:3's last-days mockers), and pointing the finger is Isaiah 58:9's; no single verse is demonstrable.
provenance.significance: Psalm 1 is six verses long and three of them are in this dream. The scornful sit in a seat (1:1) — the Book of Mormon's building is full of people sitting apart and deriding. The righteous man is 'like a tree planted by the rivers of water' bringing forth fruit (1:3) — the tree and the river of 8:10-13. And 'the way of the ungodly shall perish' (1:6) — 8:28's 'they fell away into forbidden paths, and were lost.' No phrase is reproduced anywhere, which is why this is recorded at moderate; but if the dream has a single Old Testament template rather than a set of borrowed props, Psalm 1 is it.

links.note: 'They were in the attitude of mocking and pointing their fingers towards those which had come at, and were partaking of the fruit.' Proposed as the dream's psalm rather than as this verse's source. The case is cumulative and stated under significance: Psalm 1's three images — the seat of the scornful, the tree by the water bearing fruit, the way of the ungodly that perishes — are the dream's three parties, and they arrive in Psalm 1's own order across 8:13, 8:27 and 8:28.
links.whyNot: Not one word is shared, at any of the three points. A reader who wants verbal evidence has none here, and the Sermon on the Mount (8:20, 8:26) and Revelation 22 (8:13) already account for the landscape without the Psalm. Recorded because the pattern is worth someone's testing, and flagged so that it can be struck if it does not hold.

pericopes.text: And after that they had tasted of the fruit, they were ashamed, because of those that were scoffing at them; and they fell away into forbidden paths, and were lost.
And now I, Nephi, do not speak all the words of my father.

But, to be short in writing: Behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down, and partook of the fruit of the tree.
And he also saw other multitudes, feeling their way towards that great and spacious building.
And it came to pass that many were drowned in the depths of the fountain; and many were lost from his view, wandering in strange roads.

links.text: But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.

provenance.other: 'Drowned in the depth' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 18:6 is about causing others to stumble, and the drowning in it is the punishment of the one who does the causing. In the dream the drowning happens to the stumblers themselves — 'many were drowned in the depths of the fountain' — while the people who caused it are in the building overhead, mocking. Nephi's later reading of the water as hell (15:26-29) is the Book of Mormon's own, and Matthew 18:6 is where the KJV puts a drowning in the depths on the wrong side of the moral ledger from where the dream puts it.

links.note: 'Many were drowned in the depths of the fountain; and many were lost from his view, wandering in strange roads.' The drowning phrase is a KJV singleton; the wandering is Jeremiah 18:15's 'to walk in paths, in a way not cast up', which is the prophets' image for a road that goes nowhere. Held at moderate because the phrase is short and the two texts assign the drowning to different parties.

pericopes.text: And great was the multitude that did enter into that strange building. And after that they did enter into that building, they did point the finger of scorn at me, and those that were partaking of the fruit also; but we heeded them not.
These are the words of my father: For as many as heeded them, had fallen away.
And Laman and Lemuel partook not of the fruit, saith my father.

And it came to pass that after my father had spoken all the words of his dream or vision, which were many, he said unto us, because of these things which he saw in a vision, he exceedingly feared for Laman and Lemuel; yea, he feared lest they should be cast off from the presence of the Lord;

and he did exhort them then with all the feeling of a tender parent, that they would hearken to his words, in that, perhaps the Lord would be merciful to them, and not cast them off; yea, my father did preach unto them.

links.text: As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children,

provenance.alternative: A father exhorting his children tenderly requires no source, and 'tender parent' is not a KJV phrase.
provenance.significance: 1 Thessalonians 2:7-11 is the KJV's one passage that pairs exhortation explicitly with parental tenderness on both sides — 'gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children' at 2:7, and 'we exhorted … as a father doth his children' at 2:11. 1 Nephi 8:37 is that pairing in a sentence: 'he did exhort them then with all the feeling of a tender parent.' The Book of Mormon's word is 'parent' rather than father or nurse, which is what a writer produces who has both halves of the Pauline figure in mind at once.

links.note: 'He did exhort them then with all the feeling of a tender parent, that they would hearken to his words.' Recorded on the collocation — the verb 'exhort' governed by a parental simile — which the KJV has at 1 Thessalonians 2:11 and effectively nowhere else. The chapter closes as it opened, with a father speaking to sons who will not hear him; see 8:2 for the Genesis 37:9 dream formula that started it.

pericopes.text: And after that he had preached unto them, and also prophesied unto them of many things, he bade them to keep the commandments of the Lord; and he did cease speaking unto them.
And all these things did my father see, and hear, and speak, as he dwelt in a tent, in the valley of Lemuel; and also a great many more things, which cannot be written upon these plates.

links.text: And Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.

provenance.other: 'Tent in the valley' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The chapter opens by placing the whole of Lehi's vision inside a formula: a patriarch dwelling in a tent in a named valley. Genesis 26:17 is the KJV's only instance of that exact geography, and Genesis 26:25 — eight verses later — is one of the two verses that gave 1 Nephi 2:6-7 its tent-and-altar pair. The Book of Mormon returns to the same page of Genesis whenever it needs to say where Lehi is.

links.note: 'As he dwelt in a tent, in the valley of Lemuel.' The phrase is a KJV singleton and the tent-dwelling formula has been running since 2:15. Recorded at moderate: the three words are common individually and their combination could be arrived at independently by a narrative that has already committed to tents and valleys. The verse's second half — 'a great many more things, which cannot be written upon these plates' — is the John 21:25 colophon again (see 6:3).

pericopes.text: And now, as I have spoken concerning these plates, behold, they are not the plates upon which I make a full account of the history of my people; for the plates upon which I make a full account of my people, I have given the name of Nephi; wherefore, they are called the plates of Nephi, after mine own name; and these plates also, are called the plates of Nephi.
Nevertheless, I have received a commandment of the Lord, that I should make these plates, for the special purpose that there should be an account engraven of the ministry of my people.

Upon the other plates should be engraven an account of the reign of the Kings, and the wars, and contentions of my people; wherefore, these plates are, for the more part, of the ministry; and the other plates are, for the more part, of the reign of the Kings, and the wars, and contentions of my people.
Wherefore, the Lord hath commanded me to make these plates, for a wise purpose in him; which purpose, I know not.

links.text: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.

provenance.alternative: Professed ignorance of God's reasons is the commonest of pious formulas; Isaiah 55:8 and Romans 11:33 say it more famously and neither is reproduced either.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 29:29 is the KJV's formal statement of the division 1 Nephi 9:5 acts on: God keeps his reasons, and what is disclosed is disclosed so that it can be transmitted to children. Nephi is obeying an instruction whose purpose is withheld from him, and doing it by making a second record for someone else to read — which is Deuteronomy's 'belong unto us and to our children for ever' as a task rather than a doctrine.

links.note: 'The Lord hath commanded me to make these plates, for a wise purpose in him; which purpose, I know not.' Nothing is reproduced. Recorded because the sentence is not merely modest — it is a formal statement about the distribution of knowledge between God and a scribe, which is what Deuteronomy 29:29 legislates, and because 9:6 immediately supplies the other half ('the Lord knoweth all things'). The verse is also the Book of Mormon's own explanation for the small plates, which is a claim about its transmission and not only about providence.
links.whyNot: Zero verbal contact and a commonplace sentiment. The link stands or falls on whether the reader thinks 9:5-6 is making Deuteronomy's distinction rather than simply expressing humility.

pericopes.text: But the Lord knoweth all things, from the beginning; wherefore, he prepareth a way to accomplish all his works among the children of men; for behold, he hath all power unto the fulfilling of all his words. And thus it is. Amen.

links.text: Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.

provenance.other: 'All his works from the beginning' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Acts 15:18 is a single sentence, James's closing remark at the Jerusalem council.
provenance.significance: Nephi has just said he does not know the purpose of what he has been told to do; the next sentence answers with the one KJV verse that asserts God's complete foreknowledge of his own works. Acts 15:18 is spoken at the council that decides the terms on which Gentiles enter the covenant — a decision James justifies by saying that God knew all along — and 1 Nephi 9:6 uses it to justify a record whose purpose its own maker does not know. Both are appeals to a plan visible only from the other end. The plates of Nephi are the Book of Mormon's own account of why it exists in two versions, and the sentence that closes the account is James's.

links.note: 'But the Lord knoweth all things, from the beginning; wherefore, he prepareth a way to accomplish all his works among the children of men; for behold, he hath all power unto the fulfilling of all his words.' Two elements of Acts 15:18 are reproduced — God's knowledge, and 'all his works from the beginning', a KJV singleton — and 'he prepareth a way' repeats Nephi's own formula from 3:7. The chapter's last verse is thus a compound of the book's borrowed doctrine of providence and its own catchphrase.

pericopes.text: And now I, Nephi, proceed to give an account upon these plates of my proceedings, and my reign and ministry; wherefore, to proceed with mine account, I must speak somewhat of the things of my father, and also of my brethren.
For behold, it came to pass that after my father had made an end of speaking the words of his dream, and also of exhorting them to all diligence, he spake unto them concerning the Jews:

How that after they were destroyed, yea, even that great city Jerusalem; and that many were carried away captive into Babylon; that according to the own due time of the Lord, they should return again; yea, even be brought back out of captivity; and after they are brought back out of captivity, to possess again the land of their inheritance.
Yea, even six hundred years from the time that my father left Jerusalem, a Prophet would the Lord God raise up among the Jews; yea, even a Messiah; or, in other words, a Saviour of the world.

links.text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15-18 → KJV → Book of Mormon (mediation undecided here; see 1 Nephi 22:20)
provenance.other: 'Saviour of the world' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 4:42 and 1 John 4:14. Note the 1830 spelling 'Saviour', which is the King James spelling; 1920 modernized it to 'Savior'.
provenance.alternative: Whether the raise-up-a-prophet formula reaches 1 Nephi 10:4-5 from Deuteronomy 18:15 or from Acts 3:22 cannot be decided at this verse: Deuteronomy has 'The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet', Acts has 'A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you', and 1 Nephi 10:4 has 'a Prophet would the Lord God raise up', which matches neither pronoun. The test is deferred to 22:20, where the passage is quoted at length.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 18:15-18 is the Book of Mormon's charter text and 1 Nephi 10:4-5 is its first full statement here. Lehi's Messiah is announced under Deuteronomy's title, and the verse then translates it twice — 'a Messiah; or, in other words, a Saviour of the world', the second phrase being one that exists in the KJV only in the Johannine literature. The prophet promised to Moses is glossed with a title from John.

links.note: 'A Prophet would the Lord God raise up among the Jews; yea, even a Messiah; or, in other words, a Saviour of the world.' The double gloss is the interesting part. Deuteronomy's promise is turned into a Messiah and then into a Saviour of the world, a phrase the KJV has twice and only in John and 1 John. The mediation call is explicitly left open here and taken at 22:20.

pericopes.text: And he also spake concerning the prophets: How great a number had testified of these things, concerning this Messiah, of which he had spoken, or this Redeemer of the world.
Wherefore, all mankind was in a lost and in a fallen state; and ever would be, save they should rely on this Redeemer.
And he spake also, concerning a prophet, which should come before the Messiah, to prepare the way of the Lord;

yea, even he should go forth and cry in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, and make his paths straight; for there standeth one among you whom ye know not; and he is mightier than I, whose shoe’s latchet I am not worthy to unloose. And much spake my father concerning this thing.

links.text: John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not;

provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:3 — 'The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'
provenance.route: Isaiah 40:3 → the Synoptic citation form (Matthew 3:3 / Mark 1:3 / Luke 3:4) + John 1:26-27 + Matthew 3:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The Old Testament and New Testament forms of Isaiah 40:3 diverge in the second half. Isaiah reads 'make straight in the desert a highway for our God'; all three Synoptic quotations read 'make his paths straight'. 1 Nephi 10:8 reads 'make his paths straight'. Separately: 'whose shoe's latchet' — singular, possessive — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:27; Mark 1:7 and Luke 3:16 read 'the latchet of whose shoes'. And 'is mightier than I' in that word order is Matthew 3:11's.
provenance.significance: This is the densest verse in 1 Nephi and the clearest mediation case in the book. One sentence, put in the mouth of a prophet six hundred years before John the Baptist, fuses four New Testament verses: the Synoptic form of Isaiah 40:3 (not Isaiah's own), John 1:26 verbatim for nine words, John 1:27's singular 'shoe's latchet' rather than Mark's or Luke's plural, and Matthew 3:11's 'mightier than I'. Every point at which the KJV offers a choice between two wordings, 1 Nephi 10:8 takes the New Testament's — and where the New Testament itself offers a choice, it takes John's. The next two verses continue: Bethabara at 10:9 (a place-name unique to John 1:28), the Lamb of God at 10:10 (John 1:29). Lehi's prophecy of John the Baptist is a cento of the Fourth Gospel's first chapter.

links.note: 'Yea, even he should go forth and cry in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, and make his paths straight; for there standeth one among you whom ye know not; and he is mightier than I, whose shoe's latchet I am not worthy to unloose.' Two runs of nine and ten words are reproduced verbatim, and the machine stream ranked John 1:26 and 1:27 first and second in the chapter (rarity 5.33 and 4.83). The combined verbatim material comfortably exceeds Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though it is assembled from four verses rather than continuous in one; whether he counts it among his thirty-six long quotations cannot be checked, since the itemized list is unobtainable (PLAN §4.1). Recorded at 'certain'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 10.8 (Isaiah 40:3; Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:2-3; Luke 3:4; Matthew 3:11; Mark 1:7; Luke 3:16; John 1:26-27)

pericopes.text: And my father saith that he should baptise in Bethabara, beyond Jordan; and he also spake, that he should baptise with water; yea, even that he should baptise the Messiah with water.

links.text: These things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing.

provenance.other: 'Bethabara' occurs in exactly one verse of the King James Bible, John 1:28, and the reading itself is a textual variant: the majority of Greek manuscripts and every modern critical edition read Bethany, not Bethabara. The King James translators followed the Textus Receptus here.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest single piece of evidence in 1 Nephi for the project's central claim, and it is strong precisely because it is a proper noun. A place-name that exists nowhere in scripture except one King James verse, and exists there because of a manuscript reading the King James translators happened to adopt, is spoken by a prophet in Arabia in 600 BC. Compare 10:8's 'make his paths straight' and 10:10's Lamb of God: the whole passage is John 1 in sequence, and this verse is the point at which the dependence stops being a matter of judgment. The 1830 spells the verb 'baptise', where the KJV has 'baptize'; 1920 corrected it back toward the KJV, which is the opposite of the usual direction (CONVENTIONS §8).

links.note: 'And my father saith that he should baptise in Bethabara, beyond Jordan.' Four words, one of them a proper noun found in a single KJV verse and found there on a contested reading. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations; catalogued as a quotation, and as the chapter's decisive datum, because rarity here is absolute rather than statistical.

pericopes.text: And after that he had baptised the Messiah with water, he should behold and bear record, that he had baptised the Lamb of God, which should take away the sins of the world.

links.text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon reads 'the sins of the world', plural; the KJV reads 'the sin of the world', singular, at John 1:29 and again at 1:36's shorter form. The plural is the only alteration.
provenance.significance: 'The Lamb of God' becomes the Book of Mormon's dominant title for Christ from here to the end of 1 Nephi — chapters 11 to 14 use it more than fifty times — and it enters the book in John 1:29's exact clause, three verses after Bethabara and two after John 1:26-27. The whole of Lehi's prophecy at 10:7-10 is the first chapter of John's Gospel read in order: the forerunner, the one standing unknown among them, the latchet, the place, the Lamb, and the bearing of record (John 1:34). Whatever else is going on in this book, this passage is a reading of John 1.

links.note: 'He should behold and bear record, that he had baptised the Lamb of God, which should take away the sins of the world.' John 1:29's clause with the noun pluralized and the tense shifted to prophecy; 'bear record' is John 1:34's own verb for what the Baptist then does. The 1830's 'which' where 1920 reads 'who' preserves the KJV relative.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that after my father had spoken these words, he spake unto my brethren concerning the Gospel, which should be preached among the Jews; and also, concerning the dwindling of the Jews in unbelief. And after that they had slain the Messiah which should come, and after that he had been slain, he should rise from the dead, and should make himself manifest, by the Holy Ghost, unto the Gentiles.

links.text: That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should shew light unto the people, and to the Gentiles.

provenance.other: A seven-word run — 'should rise from the dead, and should' — with 'the Gentiles' following in both.
provenance.significance: Acts 26:22-23 is Paul before Agrippa summarizing what he preaches as 'none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come': Christ suffering, rising first from the dead, and shewing light to the Gentiles. That is precisely the claim 1 Nephi 10:11 makes for Lehi — a pre-Christian prophet stating the gospel in outline — and it states it in Paul's own summary sentence. The Book of Mormon is using the New Testament's own description of Old Testament prophecy as the content of an Old Testament prophecy.

links.note: 'After that they had slain the Messiah which should come, and after that he had been slain, he should rise from the dead, and should make himself manifest, by the Holy Ghost, unto the Gentiles.' The elements and their order are Acts 26:23's — suffering, resurrection, manifestation to the Gentiles — with the seven-word run in the middle. Note the third element in 1 Nephi is 'the dwindling of the Jews in unbelief', which is Romans 11's premise and prepares the olive tree of 10:12.

pericopes.text: Yea, even my father spake much concerning the Gentiles, and also concerning the House of Israel: That they should be compared like unto an olive tree, whose branches should be broken off, and should be scattered upon all the face of the earth.

links.text: For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?

provenance.other: 'Natural branches' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:21 and 11:24. The olive-tree allegory of branches broken off, a wild stock grafted in, and the natural branches grafted back exists in the Bible only at Romans 11. 'Scattered upon all the face of the earth' is Ezekiel 34:6's, and occurs in one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Romans 11 is the Book of Mormon's master allegory. It supplies 10:12's broken branches, 10:14's natural branches grafted in, the whole of Nephi's explanation at 15:7-16, and eventually the seventy-seven verses of Jacob 5, which is the allegory expanded into a parable. Paul's argument is that Israel's unbelief is temporary and instrumental — 'blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in' (11:25) — and 1 Nephi 10:14 reproduces the sequence and even the term: 'after the Gentiles had received the fulness of the Gospel, the natural branches … should be grafted in'. Paul's 'fulness of the Gentiles' has become the 'fulness of the Gospel', and the fulness phrase itself is Romans 15:29's.

links.note: 'They should be compared like unto an olive tree, whose branches should be broken off, and should be scattered upon all the face of the earth.' Romans 11:17's broken branches, Romans 11:24's natural branches at 10:14, and the grafting in both — against Ezekiel 34:6, which supplies the scattering in an eight-word run. Held at high rather than certain because no continuous clause is reproduced; the case is the allegory, which is Paul's property in scripture, plus the two-verse phrase 'natural branches'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at 1 Ne 15.12 (Romans 11:16-24), for the same allegory at Nephi's exposition

pericopes.text: Wherefore, he said, it must needs be that we should be led with one accord, into the land of promise, unto the fulfilling of the word of the Lord: That we should be scattered upon all the face of the earth.

And after that the House of Israel should be scattered, they should be gathered together again; or, in fine, that after the Gentiles had received the fulness of the Gospel, the natural branches of the olive tree, or the remnants of the House of Israel, should be grafted in, or come to the knowledge of the true Messiah, their Lord and their Redeemer.

And after this manner of language did my father prophesy and speak unto my brethren; and also, many more things, which I do not write in this book; for I have written as many of them, as were expedient for me, in mine other book.
And all these things of which I have spoken, was done, as my father dwelt in a tent, in the valley of Lemuel.

And it came to pass that after I, Nephi, having heard all the words of my father, concerning the things which he saw in a vision; and also the things which he spake by the power of the Holy Ghost; which power, he received by faith on the Son of God. And the Son of God was the Messiah, which should come. And it came to pass that I, Nephi, was desirous also, that I might see, and hear, and know of these things, by the power of the Holy Ghost, which is the gift of God unto all those who diligently seek him, as well in times of old as in the time that he should manifest himself unto the children of men;
for he is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever; and the way is prepared from the foundation of the world, if it so be that they repent and come unto him;

links.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.other: 'The same yesterday' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the whole seven-word formula 'the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever' is unique to it. The 1830 hyphenates 'to-day'.
provenance.significance: Hebrews continues to be a governing source for this book: 11:8, 11:9 and 11:13 in chapter 2 and 5, 11:29 in chapter 4, and now 13:8. The formula becomes one of the Book of Mormon's standing arguments — it is the premise of the claim that revelation and miracle did not cease — and it is used that way here, to license Nephi's request in the previous verse for the same experience his father had, 'as well in times of old as in the time that he should manifest himself'. The immutability of God is the warrant for the continuity of revelation, which is Hebrews 13:8 pressed into service as an epistemology.
